\hypertarget{involvement}{%
\subsection{Involvement}\label{involvement}}

Two overarching frameworks in this stream of research are:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Elaboration LIkelihood Model \citep{petty1979}
\item
  Heuristic-Systematic Model H\citep{chaiken1980}
\end{enumerate}

Involvement as a key moderator in advertising effectiveness

From the ELM by \citep{petty1986} by use the word ``motivation'' in place of involvement. And if you use the term ``motivation'', reviewers are less likely to fight with you since involvement is so fragmented

For review and operationalization, check \citep{muehling1993} (preferable) or \citep{andrews1990} and famous scale is \citep{zaichkowsky1985a}

Possible manipulation of involvement:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  ego-involvement: how a product is relevant to you (e.g., pick a free product for you, or for others)
\end{itemize}

Involvement roughly means ``How deeply you are as a consumer wants to think about a product,''

Motivation (2) \textbf{Opportunity} (kinda under ability in the original ELM, we as marketers separate this factor) (3) Ability are necessary for elaboration likelihood model \citep{petty1983}

Defensive processing is not fully captured under the ELM model: Motivation: not the desire to think, but also the desire to find out the truth, assuming that consumers want to find out the truth.

Involvement vs.~Engagement:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  According to \citep{greenwald1984} (p.~583), define audience involvement and actor involvement (should be called engagement).
\end{itemize}

\citep{greenwald1984}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  derived from Sherif \& Hovland (1961) Social Judgment (ego-involvement)
\item
  Enduring involvement vs.~situational involvement (Houston \& Rothschild, 1977) (A Paradigm for Research on Consumer Involvement)
\item
  Four levels of involvement:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
  \item
    Preattention: little capacity
  \item
    Focal attention: modest capacity to decipher the message
  \item
    Comprehension: more capacity to analyze the message
  \item
    Elaboration: most capacity to integrate the message into the audience's knowledge.
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  Antecedents: Situational involvement
\item
  Consequences:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Under high involvement: communication can modify beliefs
  \item
    Under low involvement: communication affect perceptions, and can gradually be persuasive after repeated exposure.
  \item
    Under ego-involvement: high involvement is more resistance to persuasion.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Processes of involvement:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    High involvement creates link between new info to previous experience or attitude
  \item
    differentiate high vs.~involvement by central vs.~peripheral routs to persuasion \citep{petty1986}
  \item
    Mitchell (1979) equates high involvement to arousal/drive
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Involvement stems from

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Actor (participant) or audience (observer)
  \item
    Distinction: Attentional capacity and attentional arousal

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Arousal = ``a state of wakefulness, general preparation, or excitement that facilitates the performance of well-leaned response.'' (p.~583)
    \item
      Capacity (also known as effort by Kahneman (1973)) = '' a limited resource that must be used to focus on a specific task and that is needed in increasing amounts as the cognitive complexity of a task increases.'' (p.~583)
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Levels of processing: influences long-term memories
  \item
    Principles for the control of involvement:

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Bottom-up (data-driven) processing
    \item
      Top-down (concept-driven) processing
    \item
      Competence (data) limitation
    \item
      Capacity (resource) limitation
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Effects of involvement

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Immediate Effects: ``analyze codes produced by prior processing''
    \item
      Enduring Effects

      \begin{itemize}
      \item
        Preattention: no definitive conclusion
      \item
        Focal attention: (1) Familiar stimuli could be identified as separated objects and (2) Unfamiliar stimuli primes sensory memory traces
      \item
        Comprehension: create traces at the propositional level of representation
      \item
        Elaboration: ``substantial freedom of memory and attitude from the specific details of th original message or its setting.''
      \end{itemize}
    \item
      Principle of higher-level dominance: the effect of the highest level of involvement is dominant in cases where the effects of different levels oppose one another.

      \begin{itemize}
      \item
        Both routes can happen at the same time
      \item
        deeper thinking, play judgment will dominate the net results (weights on whatever route is higher)
      \end{itemize}
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\citep{petty1983}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  provides evidence for the two routes to persuasion

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Central route: long-lasting and predictive of behavior
  \item
    Peripheral route: associated with positive or negative cues , can be temporary and unpredictive of behavior.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Argument quality influences attitudes more under high than low involvement
\item
  Product endorsers (celebrities vs.~joe) influences attitudes more under low than high involvement
\item
  Can use this as an example of (1) message content, and (2) executional cues (e.g., endorsers) can influence persuasiveness.
\end{itemize}

\citep{batra1990}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Mood affects cognitive elaboration, bias the argument quality, peripherally affect brand attitudes.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Positive moods reduces elaboration
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\citep{macinnis2002}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Under ELM, for the endorsers to have an effect, customers have to have some motivation (require some levels of cognition), while affective processing does not require any motivation. Hence, for consumers have higher ability (know about products because it's mature).
\item
  For mature brands, affectively based executional cues can induce sales
\item
  Advertisement with positive feelings induces sales
\end{itemize}

\citep{schivinski2016}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Propose consumers' engagement scales (in the context of social media)
\item
  Three dimensions of consumer's engagement based on previous research \citet{muntinga2011}

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Consumption (e.g., using)
  \item
    Contribution: (e.g., liking or sharing, participating)
  \item
    Creation: (e.g., posting, producing contents)
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

McQuarrie (1998): Meta analysis

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Lab experiments (in advertising context) are different from real-world phenomenon because:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Forcing exposure
  \item
    Failing to measure choice
  \item
    does not consider competitive ads, decay, repeated exposures or mature/familiar brands.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\citep{muehling1993}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  A review on involvement in advertising research
\item
  See figure 1 (p.~43) for involvement conceptualization
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{visual-cues}{%
\subsection{Visual Cues}\label{visual-cues}}

\citet{chu2021}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Prestigious brands whose brand image is associated with status and luxury, consumers' attitude toward the product becomes more favorable and their willingness to pay a premium for the product grows as the distance between the visual representations of the product and the consumer increases.
\item
  Popular brands whose brand image is associated with broad appeal and social connectedness, the closer the distance, the more favorable is consumers' attitude and the higher their willingness to pay a premium.
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{deceptive-advertising}{%
\subsection{Deceptive Advertising}\label{deceptive-advertising}}

Regulatory reports of deceptive advertising have negative impact on stock market performance, but brand reputation can mitigate this negative effect \citep{wiles2010}

\citep{rao2022}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Fake news advertising are those that ``mimics the format of its surrounding news content in both digital and print media, promotional segments aired on news programs without disclousre to the public.'' (p.~534)
\item
  Research question: What happens when the fake news ad path is shutdown?
\item
  Data:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Browsing data: comScore
  \item
    Purchase data: Ripoff Report, Complaints Board
  \item
    Ad spend: Neilsen AdSpend data
  \item
    keep only first visits.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Total site visits = organic visits + fake news ad referrals + regular ad referrals.
\end{itemize}

\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_{merchant} &= Q_{org} + Q_{fn} + Q_{reg} \\
Q_{org} &= \alpha_{org} + \gamma_1^{fn} Ad_{fn} + \gamma_1^{reg} Ad_{reg} \\
Q_{fn} &= \alpha_{fn} Ad_{fn} + \gamma_2^{reg} Ad_{reg} I(Ad_{fn} > 0) \\
Q_{reg} &= \alpha_{reg} Ad_{reg} + \gamma_3^{fn} Ad_{fn} I(Ad_{reg} > 0)
\end{aligned}
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(fn\) = fake news
\item
  \(reg\) = regular advertising
\item
  \(Q\) = demand
\item
  \(\alpha\) = direct effect
\item
  \(\gamma\) = spillover effect
\item
  Two effects of interest of fake news

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Treatment Effect: directly to \(Q_{fn}\), spillover to organic searchers \(\gamma_1^{fn}\) or regular ad referrals \(\gamma_3^{fn}\)
  \item
    Selection Effect: In the absence of fake news, use other channels (substitution effect), 2 segments

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Those who will use other channels (e.g., regular)
    \item
      Those who will stop
    \item
      In the presence of fake news,
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Results

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Fake news ads and regular ads are substitutes (i.e., increase in regular ad referrals after FTC shutdown)
  \item
    Probability of a merchant receiving a complaint declines by 8\% after the FTC shutdown (somewhat mechanistically)
  \item
    The selection effect is small (i.e., substitution to the regard ad channel is dominated by the decline in organic demand + fake news ad referrals)
  \item
    Supply side: no change in spend, duration and impressions from the customers, or new fake news ad campaigns from merchants.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Robustness

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Negative publicity (from the press) does not explain visits reduction.
  \item
    Google might change algorithm because of the FTC shutdown. Hard to know. Hence, claim that the measured decline is the upper bound of the true impact of the FTC regulations.
  \item
    Might consider using logistic regression in rare events data here \citep{king2001logistic} (but this is a borderline case since they have 95\% 0, whereas rare events are usually 99\% 0).
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{entropy}{%
\subsection{Entropy}\label{entropy}}

Most of the examples are taken from \texttt{philentropy} package in R, which can be accessed via this \href{https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/philentropy/vignettes/Information_Theory.html}{link}

\hypertarget{discrete-entropy}{%
\subsubsection{Discrete Entropy}\label{discrete-entropy}}

If \(\mathbf{p}_X = (p_{x1},p_{x2},...,p_{xn})\) is the probability distribution of the discrete random variable X with \(P(X = x) = p_{xi}\). Then, the \textbf{entropy} of the distribution is \citep{Shannon_1948}

\[
H(\mathbf{p}_X) = -\sum_{x_i} p_{xi}\log_2 p_{xi}
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  entropy unit is \textbf{bits}, and \(H(p) \in [0,1]\) and max at \(p = 0.5\)
\item
  or the unit is \textbf{nats} (\(log_e\))
\item
  or the unit is \textbf{dits} (\(log_{10}\))
\end{itemize}

In general, if you have different bases, you can convert between units. Given bases a and b

\[
\log_a k = \log_a b \times log_b k 
\]

where \(\log_a b\) is a constant.

Generalize

\[
H_b(X) = log_b a \times H_a(X)
\]

Equivalently,

\[
H(X) = E(\frac{1}{\log p(x)})
\]

Entropy is the measure of how much information gained from learning the value of X \citep[pp.262]{Zwillinger_1995}. Entropy depends on the distribution of X.

\hfill\break
Example:

If X has 2 values, then \(\mathbf{p}= (p,1-p)\) and

\[
H(\mathbf{p}_X ) = H(p,1-p) = -p \log_2 p - (1-p) \log_2 (1-p)
\]

which is known as binary entropy function

Plot of p vs.~H(p) where max of \(H(\mathbf{p}_X) = \log_2 n\) when \(X \sim U\)

\hypertarget{mutual-information}{%
\subsubsection{Mutual Information}\label{mutual-information}}

If X and Y are two discrete random variables and \(\mathbf{p}_{X \times Y}\) is the their joint distribution, the \textbf{mutual information} (i.e., learning of a value of X gives information about the value of Y) of X and Y is

\[
I(X,Y) = I(Y,X) = H(\mathbf{p}_X)+ H(\mathbf{p}_Y)- H(\mathbf{p}_{X \times Y})
\]

where \(I(X,Y) \ge 0\) and \(I(X,Y) = 0\) iff X and Y are independent (information about X gives no information about Y).

Equivalently,

\[
MI(X,Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m P(x_i, y_j) \times \log_b (\frac{P(x_i,y_j)}{P(x_i) \times P(y_j)})
\]

Properties:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(I(X;X) = H(X)\) known as self-information
\item
  \(I(X;Y) \ge 0\) with equality iff \(X \perp Y\)
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{relative-entropy}{%
\subsubsection{Relative Entropy}\label{relative-entropy}}

The measure of the distance between distribution p and q is called \textbf{relative entropy}, denoted by \(D(p ||q)\)

Equivalently, it measures the inefficiency of assuming distribution q when the true distribution is p.

The relative entropy between p(x) and q(x) is

\[
D(p||q) = \sum_x p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(X)}
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(D(p||q) \ge 0\) and equality iff \(p = q\)
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{joint-entropy}{%
\subsubsection{Joint-Entropy}\label{joint-entropy}}

\[
H(X,Y) = - \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^m P(x_i, y_j) \times \log_b(P(x_i,y_j))
\]

\FunctionTok{JE}\NormalTok{(P\_xy) }\CommentTok{\# Joint{-}Entropy}

\[
H(Y|X) = - \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^m P(x_i, y_j) \times \log_b(\frac{P(x_i)}{P(x_i,y_j)})
\]

\end{verbatim}

Relation among entropy measures

\[
H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X) = H(Y) + H(X|Y)
\]

Properties:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Chain rule: \(H(X_1, ..., X_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n H(X_i | X_{i-1},...,X_1)\)
\item
  \(0 \le H(Y|X) \le H(Y)\) Information on X does not increase the entropy measure of Y
\item
  If \(X \perp Y\), then \(H(Y|X) = H(Y); H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y)\)
\item
  \(H(X) \le log |n_X|\) where \(n_X\) = number of elements in X
\item
  \(H(X) = \log (n_X)\) iff \(X \sim U\)
\item
  \(H(X_1,...,X_n) \le \sum_i^n H(X_i)\)
\item
  \(H(X_1,...,X_n) = \sum_i^n H(X_i)\) iff \(X_i\)'s are mutually independent.
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{continuous-entropy}{%
\subsubsection{Continuous Entropy}\label{continuous-entropy}}

If X is a continuous variable, its entropy is

\[
h(\mathbf{X}) = - \int_{R^d} p(\mathbf{x})\log p(\mathbf{x}) dx
\]

where d is the dimension of X.

If X and Y are continuous random variables with density functions \(p(\mathbf{x})\) and \(q(\mathbf{y})\), the relative entropy is

\[
H(X,Y) = \int_{R^d} p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} dx
\]

More advance analysis can be access \href{https://elife-asu.github.io/rinform/\#4_time_series_measures}{here}

\hypertarget{divergence}{%
\subsection{Divergence}\label{divergence}}

Three metrics for divergence can be found \href{https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/philentropy/vignettes/Information_Theory.html}{here}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Kullback-Leibler
\item
  Jensen-Shannon
\item
  Generalized Jensen-Shannon
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{channel-capacity}{%
\subsection{Channel Capacity}\label{channel-capacity}}

The information channel capacity of a discrete memoryless channel is

\[
C = \max_{p(x)} I(X;Y)
\]

which is the highest rate use at which information can be sent without much error.\\
More information can be found \href{http://www.di.fc.ul.pt/~jpn/r/inf_theory/informationtheory.html}{here}

\hypertarget{sales}{%
\chapter{Sales}\label{sales}}

\citep{habel2021} found that consistent with traditional idea, having variable factor in salesperson's compensation plan will increase performance, but also introduce health hazard (more stress which results in emotional exhaustion and more sick days). In cases where salespeople have higher personal ability and more social resources, this harmful effect is mitigated.

\hypertarget{sales-from-rank}{%
\section{Sales from Rank}\label{sales-from-rank}}

\citep{chevalier2003measuring}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  use an experiment to infer demand
\item
  From low-selling books (where demand was either known or very small) and purchased large quantities (relative to their low demand)
\item
  Data from Amazon
\item
  As the ranks for the books changed, the relationship between the sales rank and demand can be inferred.
\item
  However, this is practical only to very low-selling books.
\end{itemize}

\citep{brynjolfsson2003consumer}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  With additional demand data from a book publisher, they can derive the relationship between the sales and rank.
\end{itemize}

\citep{garg2013inferring}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Without demand data, they can infer the demand data
\end{itemize}

On Apple's App Store, there are three rank list:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Top-free apps
\item
  Top-paid apps
\item
  Top-grossing apps: based on revenue generation
\end{enumerate}

Assuming a Pareto distribution

\[
d_{r_p} = b_p \times r_p^{-a_p}|1 \le 200
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(d_{r_p}\) = downloads at rank \(r_p\) in the \textbf{top-paid}
\item
  \(b_p\) = scale factor that is dependent on the total market size for iPad or iPhone apps
\item
  \(a_p\) = shape of the Pareto curve
\end{itemize}

For apps in the top-grossing list, we assume a Pareto distribution for each app (to estimate use a simple truncated OLS regression)

\[
\begin{aligned}
pd_{r_g} &= p \times d_{r_p} = b_g \times r_g^{-a_g} \\
\log(r_g) &= \frac{1}{a_g} \times \log\left( \frac{b_g}{b_p} \right) + \frac{a_p}{a_g} \times \log (r_p) - \frac{1}{a_g} \times \log(p) \\
\log(r_g) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \log(r_p) + \beta_2 \log(p)
\end{aligned}
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(p\) = product price
\item
  \(b_g\) = scale factor that is dependent on the total market size for iPad or iPhone apps
\item
  \(d_{r_p}\) = downloads of the same app in the top-paid list
\item
  Assumption: top-grossing apps generate revenue from upfront pricing only

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Free and paid apps may have additional purchasable features inside the app, but these purchases will not be included in the paid apps (which is reasonable since paid apps make most of their money from upfront prices) (p.~1256).
  \item
    It's reasonable to assume that in-app features are most common in free apps (p.~1256)
  \item
    Apps' rank and price are assumed to be independent across sectional data (even when an app appears multiple times).
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \(a_g = - 1/\beta_2\)
\item
  \(a_p = -\beta_1/\beta_2\)
\item
  \(\frac{b_g}{b_p} = \exp(-\beta_1/\beta_2)\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    To recover individual values of the scale parameters, we aggregate downloads across apps in a day (since actual downloads for an app is not available) \(D_t = \sum d_{r_p} = b_p \sum_{r=1}^N r_p^{-a_p}\)
  \item
    Using the total number of downloads of top ranked apps, the two parameters are

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      \(b_p = (\sum_{r_p=1}^N d_{r_p})/(\sum_{r_p = 1}^N r_p^{-a_p})\)
    \item
      \(b_g = \exp(-\beta_0 / \beta_1)\times (\sum_{r_p=1}^N d_{r_p})/(\sum_{r_p = 1}^N r_p^{-a_p})\)
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Data:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Apple, Appshopper (shutdown in 2021), AppAnnie (now is \href{https://www.data.ai/}{data.ai}), \href{https://www.mobilewalla.com/mobile-data}{Mobilewalla}
\item
  Period: April 2011 - May 2011
\item
  Data: 200 paid apps, 200 grossing apps and their price data.
\end{itemize}

\citep{he2020sales} On Amazon, which is a generalized results from \citep{chevalier2003measuring}

\hypertarget{customer-lifetime-value-clv}{%
\chapter{Customer Lifetime Value (CLV)}\label{customer-lifetime-value-clv}}

also known as Lifetime Value (LTV)

\href{https://media.bain.com/customer-value/home/}{Bain \& Comapny customer value model}

``A year's projected business gives a number that is normally about half of a customer's full lifetime value, although that can vary by industry.'' \citep{kumar_2007}

\citep{Kumar_2008} CLV model

\[
CLV_i = \sum_{j = T+1}^{T+N} \frac{p(Buy_{ij}=1)\times \hat{CM}_{ij}}{(1+r)^{j-T}} - \frac{\hat{MC}_{ij}}{(1-r)^{j-T}}
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(CLV_i\) = lifetime value for customer i,
\item
  \(p(Buy_{ij})\) = predicted probability that customer i will purchase in period j,
\item
  \(CM_{ij}\) = predicted contribution margin provided by customer i in period j,
\item
  \(MC_{ij}\) = predicted marketing costs directed toward customer i in period j,
\item
  \(j\) = index for time periods (semiannual or annual)
\item
  \(T\) = the end of the calibration or observation time frame (usually 1 year projection),
\item
  \(N\) = total number of prediction periods,
\item
  \(r\) = semiannual discount factor (e.g., 0.07238 \citep{Kumar_2008} = 15\% annual rate)
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{example}{%
\section{Example}\label{example}}

This example is subscription customers by \href{https://www.analyzecore.com/2018/09/19/ltv-prediction-for-a-recurring-subscription-with-r/}{Sergey Bryl'} in which he adapted model \href{https://faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2012/04/Fader_hardie_jim_07.pdf}{Fader and Hardie (2007)}

\hypertarget{referral-value-crv}{%
\section{Referral value (CRV)}\label{referral-value-crv}}

``Referrals made by customers after a referral-incentive marketing campaign can be attributed to that campaign for about a year.'' \citep{kumar_2007}. Hence, we usually count those referrals made after one year of a campaign.

2 types of referral:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Type-one referral: Would not join without referral.\\
\item
  Type-two referral: still join without referral.
\end{itemize}

\citep{kumar_2007} estimated that each customer made about half type-one and half type-two referrals.

Referral value = PV(Type-one referrals) + PV(Type-two referrals)

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  PV(type-two referrals) = the prevent value of the savings in acquisition costs.
\end{itemize}

\[
CRV_i = \sum_{t =1}^{T} \sum_{y = 1}^{n1} \frac{A_{ty} - a_{ty} - M_{ty} + ACQ1_{ty}}{(1+r)^t} + \sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{y = n1+1}^{n2} \frac{ACQ2_{ty}}{(1+r)^t}
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  T = the number of periods that will be predicted into the future (e.g., typically 1 year)
\item
  \(A_{ty}\) = the gross margin contributed by customer y who other otherwise would not have bought the product,
\item
  \(a_{ty}\) = the cost of the referral for the customer y (this is what you set up)
\item
  \(n1\) = the number of customers who would not join without the referral,
\item
  \(n2-n1\) = the number of customers who would have joined anyway,
\item
  \(M_{ty}\) = the marketing costs needed to retain the referred customers,
\item
  r = semiannual discount factor (\citep{Kumar_2008} used .07238 = 15\% annual rate)
\item
  \(ACQ1_{ty}\) = the savings in acquisition costs from customers who would not join without the referral,
\item
  \(ACQ2_{ty}\) = the savings in acquisition cost from customers who would have joined anyway.
\end{itemize}

Customers with high CLV does not guarantee high CRV \citep{kumar_2007}. Hence, \citep{kumar_2007} proposed the customer value matrix

\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{images/customer_value_matrix.jpg}

\hypertarget{celebrity-endorsement}{%
\chapter{Celebrity Endorsement}\label{celebrity-endorsement}}

Based on \href{https://bookdown.org/mike/social-theory/power-distance-theory.html}{Power Distance Theory}, power distance beliefs moderates the positive effect of celebrity endorsers on evaluations of advertising \citep{Winterich_2018}

\citet{mccracken1989}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Source credibility and source attractiveness model are criticized
\item
  \textbf{Meaning transfer} model is then proposed to explain the effectiveness of celebrities as endorsers can be traced to cultural meaning (meaning from celebrity to product to consumer)
\item
  celebrity endorsers are ``individuals who enjoy public recognition and use this recognition on behalf of a consumer good by appearing with it in an advertisement.'' (p.310)
\item
  Mode of endorsement:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    explicit mode
  \item
    implicit mode
  \item
    imperative mode
  \item
    copresent mode
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Original model contends expertness and trustworthiness affect message effectiveness

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Expertness = ``perceived ability of the source to make valid assertions''
  \item
    Trustworthiness = ``perceived willingness of the source to make valid assertions.''
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Source attractiveness model contends familiarity, likability, similarity of the source affect message effectiveness.

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Familiarity = ``knowledge of the source through exposure''
  \item
    Likability = ``affection for the source as a result of the source's physical appearance and behavior.''
  \item
    Similarity = ``a supposed resemblance between the source and receiver of the message.''
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Cultural meaning and celebrity endorser:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Variety of the meanings: status, class, gender, age, personality, and lifestyles
  \item
    Meaning transfer:

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      Under culturally constituted world, meaning from consumer goods to consumers. Advertising is the vehicle to facilitate this transfer.
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{images/meaning transfer.png}

(p.~315)

\citet{mccracken1986}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Cultural meaning moves from culturally constituted world to goods to consumers
\item
  Instruments that facilitates this movement are:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Advertising
  \item
    The fashion system
  \item
    Four consumption rituals

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Possession ritual
    \item
      Exchange ritual
    \item
      Grooming ritual
    \item
      Divestment ritual
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{nudges}{%
\chapter{Nudges}\label{nudges}}

\citep{Garbinsky_2020} uncovers that people under save because they have positive illusion of financial responsibility (i.e., they thought they are financially more responsible than the average).

\citep{Mrkva_2021} found that choice architecture influences inequities across people. More specifically, people with the following dimensions enjoy the most benefit from nudges:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Low socioeconomic status (SES)
\item
  Low numerical ability
\item
  Low knowledge
\end{itemize}

Hence, we should use nudges to reduce SES disparities.

\hypertarget{marketing-finance-interface}{%
\chapter{Marketing-Finance Interface}\label{marketing-finance-interface}}

Review papers

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \citep{srinivasan2009, commenta2009}
\item
  \citep{edeling2016}: meta-analysis
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{images/paste-E4F43EEF.png}
\caption{Figure 1 \citep{srinivasan2009}}
\end{figure}

Market efficiency

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Weak efficiency: historical information only
\item
  Semi-strong efficiency: historical info + public info in real time
\item
  Strong Efficiency: historical info + public and private info
\end{itemize}

In marketing, the general consensus is that market efficiency holds in between its weak and semi-strong form

stock market reward firms with higher stock prices as good news about marketing becomes available and vice versa.

Stock market valuation is in sync with product-market valuation (i.e., actions that drive value in product markets should drive firm value)

Methods

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Single equation approach based on ECM: (e.g., \citep{srinivasan2009a}) recognizing random walk
\item
  Stock return response modeling
\item
  Persistence Modeling (VAR modeling)
\end{itemize}

Market-based assets are defined as those ``arise from the commingling of the firm with entities in its external environment'' \citep[p.~2]{Srivastava_1998}

Assets are ``any physical, organizational, or human attribute that enables the firm to generate and implement strategies that improve its efficiency and effectiveness in the marketplace'' \citep[p.~3]{Srivastava_1998}

Sustained value creation test

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Convertible (firms can exploit assets)
\item
  Rare
\item
  Imperfectly imitable
\item
  No perfect substitutes
\end{enumerate}

Market-based assets are: relational and intellectual.

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Relational market-based assets are ``outcomes of the relationship between a firm and key external stakeholders, including distributors, retailers, end customers, other strategic partners''. \citep{Srivastava_1998}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    For example, brand equity = relational assets between firms and their customers, while channel equity - relational assets between firms and their channel partners. Brand equity can be created from advertising and superior product functionality.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Intellectual market-based assets are ``the types of knowledge a firm possesses about the environment, such as the emerging and the potential state of market conditions and the entities in it, including competitors, customers, channels, suppliers, and social and political interest group.'' \citep{Srivastava_1998}
\end{itemize}

Intangible assets can be thought of as \citep[p.~5]{Srivastava_1998}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Stock: ``a specific amount or extent of brand equity or knowledge of customers' purchasing criteria possessed by a firm
\item
  Flow: ``the extent to which a stock of a particular asset is augmenting or decaying.''
\end{itemize}

Examples of market-based assets

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Customer relationships
\item
  Channel relationships
\item
  Partner relationships
\end{itemize}

Market-based assets ``increase shareholder value by accelerating and enhancing cash flows, lowering the volaitliity and vulnerability of cash flows, and increasing the residual value of cash flows'' \citep[p.~2]{Srivastava_1998}

\includegraphics{images/paste-93BB2912.png}

\citep[p.~2, table 1]{Srivastava_1998}

Market-based assets: 3 propositions

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The more market-based assets external entities can develop, the more satisfied and eager they are to work with the firm, and the more valuable they are to the firm.
\item
  The more market-based assets pass asset testing, the more external entities benefit.
\item
  When a company taps or leverages market-based assets to boost cash flows, shareholder value is created.
\end{enumerate}

Generating Customer Value

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{images/paste-CDAADBBC.png}
\caption{\citep[p.~9]{Srivastava_1998}}
\end{figure}

Different from tangible balance-sheet assets, intangible assets can create long-term sustained customer value by

\begin{itemize}
\item
  satisfying the four resource-based tests (knowledge and relationships pass all the tests)
\item
  adding the value-generating capability of physical assets (Marketing capabilities inherent in organizational processes, such as new product development, order fulfillment, and speed to market, cannot be generated or utilized without \textbf{knowledge} of and \textbf{relationships} with external entities, such as customers, distributors, suppliers, and other strategic partners. The successful execution of these competencies extends and enhances knowledge and relationships.)
\item
  exploiting the benefits of organizational networks (network is ``a coordinated set of knowledge sources and cooperative relationships'' where the value can be greater than the sum of its individual components \citep[p.~7]{Srivastava_1998})
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{images/paste-6C526C8B.png}
\caption{\citep[p.~8 Figure 1]{Srivastava_1998}}
\end{figure}

Asset Valuation Methods and Drivers of Shareholder Value

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Book value (bad because of historical value)
\item
  Replacement value (bad because of measurement issue)
\item
  PE (bad because of accrual accounting measure of firm performance)
\item
  shareholder value approach (current best): discounted future cash flow.

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Present value of cash flows during the value growth period and long-term residual value of the business at the end of the value growth period.
  \item
    Value of any strategy is determined by

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      \textbf{An acceleration of cash flow}s (today's money is preferred than tomorrow's - less risk)
    \item
      \textbf{An increase in the level of cash flows} (e.g., higher sales, or lower costs, working capital, fixed investments)
    \item
      \textbf{A reduction in risk associated with cash flows} (either via volatility or vulnerability of future cash flows), and firm's cost of capital
    \item
      \textbf{The residual value of the business} (long-term value is improved by larger customer base).
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Market-Based Assets and Shareholder value

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Accelerating cash flow: increasing the responsiveness of the marketplace to marketing activity

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Quicker response to ads from greater brand equity (brand awareness), faster product trial \citep{keller1993}
  \item
    Speed up product life cycle (time-to-market acceptance) from installed base and more partnership to speed to up the product adoption process\citep{robertson1993reduce}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Enhancing cash flows:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    generating higher revenues: e.g., product extension
  \item
    Lowering costs: extensions can increase market share and advertising efficiency and lower costs.
  \item
    Lowering working capital requirements: relationship marketing can increase efficiency
  \item
    Lowering fixed capital requirement: relationship marketing can increase efficiency. Networked market-based assets (from cooperative ventures - co-branding, co-marketing alliances) allow partners to leverage each other's networks including customer base.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Vulnerability and Volatility of Cash Flows

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    The vulnerability of cash flows decreases with increased customer satisfaction loyalty and retention
  \item
    Customers and channel partners relationships enhance stability in operations (from greater sharing of information, automatic ordering and replenishment, lower inventories).
  \item
    Net present value of a cash flow is enhanced with increased switching costs, and lowering of capital requirements from operation integration.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Residual Value of Cash Flows (those beyond forecast periods)

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    increase with size, loyalty and quality (purchase more) of customer base
  \item
    customer base creates barriers fro competition.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Cash flow is encouraged to be firm performance measure because of less accrual accounting problems (i.e., historical performance, not adjusted for risk, and easily manipulated)
\end{itemize}

Marketing actions (e.g, adverting, product innovation) can build long-term assets (e.g., brand equity, customer equity), in turn increase short-term profitability (e.g., increase marketing effectiveness for dollars spent on advertising) \citep{Rust_2004}

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{images/The-chain-of-marketing-productivity-Source-Rust-et-al-2004.png}

The Chain of Marketing Productivity (source \citep{Rust_2004})

Relationship between marketing and finance \citep{Srivastava_1998}

Stage 1: Market-based Assets

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Customer relationships: Brands, installed base.
\item
  Partner Relationship: channels, co-branding network.
\end{itemize}

Stage 2:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Faster Market penetration
\item
  Price premium
\item
  share premium
\item
  extensions
\item
  reduce sales/service costs
\item
  Loyalty/ Retention
\end{itemize}

Stage 3: Shareholder value:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Accelerate Cash Flows
\item
  Enhance Cash Flows
\item
  Reduce Volatility and Vulnerability of Cash flows
\item
  Enhance Residual Value of Cash Flows.
\end{itemize}

\citep{Grewal_2010, McAlister_2016, Morgan_2009} used Tobin's Q in marketing research. since it is ``forward-looking, risk-adjusted, and less easily manipulated by managers'' \citep{Wies_2019}. When probing factors affecting Tobin's Q, it was suggested to control for \textbf{financial leverage}, and \textbf{cash flows}

\citet{anderson2018} found that there is a significant improvements from increasing both business skills (marketing and finance). However, the pathway to improve profits from marketing skills is via growth focus (e.g., higher sales, more investments in products, and employees). The pathway to improve profits from the finance skills is via efficiency or cost focus. Hence, the recommendation is that marketing/sales skills have better fit for startups, while finance/accounting skills are more needed in mature companies.

\citet{cheong2021} found that advertising investments is not only beneficial in terms of customers, but also in terms of investors since it reduces stock price synchronicity (i.e., a firm stock price follows closely to its industry moving)

\citet{lacka2021} define price impact as'' the impact on the variance of stock price.'' They estimate the permanent and temporary price impacts of the firm-generated Twitter content of S\&P 500 IT firms: firm-generated tweets induce both permanent and temporary price impacts, depending on valence and subject matter. Tweets reflecting \textbf{only valence or subject matter} concerning consumer or competitor orientation only have \textbf{temporary} price impacts, while those with both attributes generate permanent price impact. Moreover, negative valence tweets about competitors generate the largest permanent price impacts.

\hypertarget{business-valuation}{%
\section{Business Valuation}\label{business-valuation}}

\citep{mccarthy2017} Valuing subscription-based business

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Use DISH network and Sirius XM Holdings data, the authors estimate the overall value of the firm (customer-based corporate valuation)
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{ma}{%
\section{M\&A}\label{ma}}

\citep{chari2009}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Acquirers of domestic targets experience bigger short- and long-term wealth benefits than offshore acquirers. Deals that diversify across borders perform poorly. Returns are higher when the target's domestic product and financial markets move independently of the acquirer's own nation. Stock markets favor developed market acquirers in emerging markets.
\item
  As developing market spreads grow, acquirer returns rise. When majority ownership is transferred, the acquirer, target, and acquirer's shareholders all enjoy stronger profits, especially in R\&D- and brand-intensive businesses where intellectual assets are significant.
\end{itemize}

\citep{bouwman2009market}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  In terms of two- and three-year buy-and-hold returns, bull market acquisitions underperform bear market acquisitions.
\item
  Managers suffer from hubris during market upswings and overestimate synergies and profits. When the market is pessimistic, managers make more cautious decisions, thus purchases are motivated by realistic prospects of beneficial synergies.
\end{itemize}

\citep{sudarsanam2003glamour}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Undervalued acquirers with high book-to-market ratios (value' acquirers) have favorable long-run returns, while overvalued acquirers with low book-to-market ratios have negative returns.
\item
  The stock market extrapolates management's ability to make solid purchases from the company's finances. ``Glamour'' acquirers' managers are generally overconfident in their ability to handle an acquisition, and their actions aren't rigorously checked. Value' acquirers, rigorously scrutinized by other stakeholders, are more cautious in appraising possible targets, leading to wiser decisions.
\end{itemize}

\citep{megginson2004}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Business similarity between merging firms is linked with positive stock performance.
\item
  Divestitures or spin-offs that dispose of non-core assets or operating divisions boost stockholder value.
\end{itemize}

\citep{harford1999corporate}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Excess cash acquisitions fail. Announcement period returns are negatively associated with an acquirer's cash.
\item
  A cash reserve eliminates external borrowing. When managers are shielded from the external market, they make irrational investment decisions.
\end{itemize}

\citep{fuller2002returns, conn2005impact}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Buyer shareholders enjoyed big gains when the target was a privately owned corporation or a parent-controlled subsidiary.
\item
  The bidder benefits from the illiquidity discount and enhanced information sharing from concentrated ownership.
\item
  Bidders using stock transfers and other non-cash means did not underperform and saw positive stock market reactions. Private target managers, who are expected to become major stakeholders in the new business, have a greater motive to supervise the bidder's management, which provides value for the bidder. Deferred tax obligations in a stock offer may lead target ownership to accept a lower price. This leads to increased shareholder returns.
\item
  A lack of awareness around private bids makes it easier for bidders to abandon discussions, reducing hubris-driven judgments. The stock market favors glamour' businesses bidding for private targets.
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{tobins-q}{%
\section{Tobin's Q}\label{tobins-q}}

Traditional Tobin's q \citep{Rao_2004}

\[
q = \frac{MVE + PS + DEBT}{TA}
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\item
  MVE = share price x number of common stock outstanding
\item
  PS = liquidating value of the firm's preferred stock
\item
  DEBT = (short-term liabilities - short-term assets) + book value of long-term debt
\item
  TA = book value of total assets
\end{itemize}

Tobin's q is scale independent. Hence, it's a good measure of relative market performance

\citep{peters2017} Peters and Taylor Total Q

\begin{itemize}
\item
  The neoclassical theory of investment can still be applied to intangible assets.
\item
  Propose a new Tobin's q proxy that accounts for intangible capital, which is called \textbf{total q}

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    = the firm's market value divided by the sum of its physical and intangible capital stocks
  \item
    Firm's intangible capital = sum of its knowledge capital and organizational capital

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      R\&D spending = an investment in knowledge capital (using the perpetual -inventory method to a firm's past R\&D to measure the replacement cost of its knowledge capital)
    \item
      Fraction of past selling, general, and administrative (SG\&A) spending is organization capital, which includes human capital, brand, customer relationship,s and distribution systems.
    \item
      A firm's total capital as the sum of its physical and intangible capital (measured at replacement cost
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Intangible capital is costlier than physical capital to adjust
\item
  \href{https://wrds-www.wharton.upenn.edu/pages/get-data/peters-and-taylor-total-q/peters-and-taylor-total-q/}{Download Data from WRDS}
\item
  Sample excludes utilities (SIC 4900-4999), financial firms (6000-6999), others (9000+), missing or non-positive book value of assets or sales, and firms with less than \$5mil in physical capital. Winsorize all regression variables at the 1\% level to remove outliers.
\end{itemize}

Proposed total q

\[
\begin{aligned}
q^{tot}_{it} &= \frac{V_{it}}{K_{it}^{phy} + K_{it}^{int}} \\
&= \frac{prcc_f \times csho + dltt + dlc- act}{ppegt + K_{it}^{int}}
\end{aligned}
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(V_{it}\) = firm's market value = outshining equity (prcc\_f times csho)+ book value of debt (dltt + dlc) - firm's current assets (act)
\item
  \(K_{it}^{phy}\) = replacement cost of physical capital = ppegt
\item
  \(K_{it}^{int}\) = replacement cost of intangible capital
\end{itemize}

Previous Tobin's q measure did not include the intangible part \citep{fazzari1987} \citep{erickson2011a}

Intangible capital can be

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Created internally

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    knowledge knowledge (e.g., patents, software): using perpetual inventory method \(G_{it} = (1- \delta_{RD}) G_{i, t-1} + RD_{it}\)

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      \(G_{it}\) = the end-of-period stock of knowledge capital (for \(G_{i0}\) can assume to be 0)
    \item
      \(\delta_{RD}\) =depreciation rate (use BEA's industry-specific R\&D depreciation rates \citep{li2018} and 15\% for missing data)
    \item
      \(RD_{it}\) = real expenditures on R\&D during the year (if missing treat as 0, \citep{lev}
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    brand capital (advertising under selling expense within SG\&A)
  \item
    human capital (employee training under general or admin expense within SG\&A)
  \item
    Others: Other Intangible Assets (intano) in Compustat
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Purchased externally

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Goodwill (not separately identifiable e.g., human capital is booked under goodwill).
  \item
    Other Intangible Asset: (e..g, patent, software if separately identifiable)
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

  \item
    Length of 10-K filings
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Data

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    XBRL from Calbench, criteria:

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      2011-2014 that filed within 150 days of the fiscal year-end
    \item
      merge with compustat
    \item
      positive sales, and non-missing common shares outstanding
    \item
      assets \textgreater{} 10 mil
    \item

    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}

\citep{hoitash2022} Firm complexity

\begin{itemize}
\item
  ARC was used to measure firm complexity

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    It can be dis aggregated to measure the complexity of specific economic activities, (e.g., derivatives or leases)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Even though \citep{loughran2020, loughran2020a} measure firm complexity using dictionary-based approach, the texts can sometimes refer to other companies' activities, whereas accounting line items belong to the focal firm
\item
  Accounting disclosures comprise the majority of economic and corporate activity. Consequently, these disclosures can reflect company complexity holistically.
\item
  Other measures of complexity: such as number of operating segments (e.g., \url{https://gist.github.com/joosti/213050de42d6e78f1634}) using BUSSEG (business segments) and OPSEG (operating segment) in compustat.
\item
  \citep{hoitash2021} find that when complexity increases, analysts struggle to create accurate forecasts.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \citep{garcia2020} find that CSR are positively correlated with greater ARC.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{privacy}{%
\chapter{Privacy}\label{privacy}}

Reviews:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Retailing: \citep{martin2020, martin2020a}
\end{itemize}

\citep{martin2016} Data privacy in marketing

Definitions of privacy

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Privacy as ``a limited access to a consumer's information'' \citep{westin1967f} with 4 substates: anonymity, solitude, reserve, and intimacy
\item
  claim to control personal information flows
\end{itemize}

Consumer info privacy: ``control of dissemination and use of consumer information including, but not limited to demographic, search history and personal profile information'' (p.~136). Examples of consumer privacy violations are unwanted marketing communication, highly targeted advertisements, online tracking.

Privacy concerns are proxies for measuring consumer privacy that is often operationalized as consumers' beliefs, attitudes, and perceptions bout their privacy (survey data) \citep{malhotra2004internet}.

Privacy paradox: the disconnect between consumers' declared privacy desires and their actual privacy policies (even though people say that they are concerned about privacy, they still hare their sensitive personal information freely).

Privacy failure (e.g., data breach, hacking intrusion, company loss company): \citep{malhotra2011evaluating, martin2017data}

Privacy can be a dimension for firms to differentiate \citep{casadesus2015competing, rust2002customer}

Privacy in society:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Federal Trade Commission (FTC) regulates consumer info privacy issues using 2 frameworks

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Notice-and-Choice Model (including Fair Info Practice Principles)
  \item
    Harm-Based Model (whether harms occurs)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  European Union (EU) Data Protection Directive is a set of consumer info privacy protections (more comprehensive than U.S.-based).

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    The default approach to address consumer information privacy concerns is still industry self-regulation (but after the article was published, EU has GDPR but nothing in the US).
  \end{itemize}
\item
  When firms lack privacy regulations, consumer demand more government intervention \citep{milberg2000}
\item
  advertising effectiveness is diminished after EU Data protection directive was implemented \citep{goldfarb2011online}
\end{itemize}

Theoretical perspectives of privacy:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Social Contract Theory: A moral contract regulates the fundamental principles and agreements between a society and an individual. Consumers believe that marketers have kept their end of the social contract when the company gives them with additional value through personalized products or monetary compensation.
\item
  Justice Theory: Procedures designed to preserve customer privacy represent the procedural justice dimension, whereas the outcome of a marketing interaction with privacy implications represents the distributive justice dimension. Fair access to and utilization of information are characteristics of procedural fairness. Fair-appearing policies can address privacy concerns.

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Theoretical outcomes of distributive justice include any benefits consumers obtain for disclosing their personal information, so jeopardizing their privacy. Common outcomes include customized goods, personalized value, faster customer-business interaction, complimentary services, and even monetary compensation.
  \item
    Parallel privacy paradox indicates that customers like the outcomes delivered by these marketers while simultaneously feeling vulnerable when releasing personal information. \citep{awad2006}
  \item
    Complex privacy policies that impede customer comprehension are perceived as less fair and, thus, decrease consumer confidence and trust in the company \citep{vail2008empirical}. Procedural privacy is about not only firms' privacy policies but also consumers' interpretation of them.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Power-Responsibility Equilibrium Theory/ Control Theory: The social obligation of the more powerful partner in a partnership is to foster a sense of equality (trust and confidence). Consumers respond defensively to perceived power inequalities (i.e., threats to their information privacy). As a result, they may withhold facts or supply false information to a company.
\item
  Social Exchange Theory: When perceived benefits exceed perceived costs, people will disclose personal information. Benefits include individualized marketing offerings or even free services (e.g., consumers regard more frequent marketing communication and targeted advertisements as a trade-off for valuable services supplied by the marketer).

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    When consumers sense greater personalization value from an information exchange, they are more likely to believe marketers have met their end of the social contract governing the transaction \citep{chellappa2005}.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Reactance Theory: Privacy concerns heighten reactance

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Some consumers fear that highly targeted and individualized marketing communications violate their privacy \citep{tucker2013}
  \item
    Ultimately, consumer responses to tailored and personalized marketing communications might appear as communication avoidance, information falsification, unfavorable word-of-mouth, and other negative behaviors \citep{white2008getting}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Behavioral Decision Theory: Consumer perceptions and behaviors about privacy are influenced by multidimensional rational calculations.
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{images/paste-55E87AE7.png}
\caption{p.~140}
\end{figure}

Consumer privacy concerns:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  ``a proxy for understanding consumers' feeling about their information privacy'' (p.~145)
\item
  Survey scales: see \citep{smith1996information}, more updated version \citep{malhotra2004internet} which includes

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    information collection
  \item
    unauthorized secondary use (internal and external)
  \item
    improper access
  \item
    error protection
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Alternatively, \citep{sheehan2000dimensions} use a somewhat similar set of dimensions

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Awareness of information collection
  \item
    Information use
  \item
    Information sensitivity
  \item
    Familiarity with entity
  \item
    Compensation
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Privacy concerns increase over time among both older and younger consumers (but more for older) \citep{goldfarb2011online}
\item
  privacy concern is a mediators of a website's personalization increasing click-through \citep{bleier2015importance}
\item
  Firm signals (e.g., privacy seals) increase consumers' willingness to reveal info, and promote positive perceptions about the org \citep{miyazaki2002internet}
\item
  The broadcast of a privacy policy reduces customer disclosure. In addition, people are inclined to share greater sensitive information when they feel that others have already done so, indicating a decreased risk of disclosure \citep{acquisti2012impact}
\item
  Privacy policy declarations boost the benevolence and integrity elements of trust, but do not increase purchase intent (p.~146)
\item
  Increased purchasing from websites with more stringent privacy practices (i.e., Customers are willing to pay more for privacy) \citep{tsai2011effect}
\end{itemize}

Trust:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  In contrast to measures to alleviate privacy concerns, which are reactive procedures, firm initiatives to increase trust serve as proactive mechanisms \citep{wirtz2009regulatory}
\item
  In situations where retailers have personalized or targeted consumer material, trust plays an important role in assuaging privacy worries \citep{aguirre2016}
\item
  People do read privacy policies, and those policies influence their trust in that firm \citep{milne2004strategies} (84\% in the sample of 2500 consumers)
\item
  \citep{martin2017data} privacy policies can be a good proxy for firms transparency and control, and they are related to firm performance and consumer behaviors.
\end{itemize}

Personalization:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Mixed effects on consumers outcome (p.~147)
\item
  Key question: Whether information was provided voluntarily or unwillingly, given marketers' ability to gather data overtly or secretly through a variety of methods.
\end{itemize}

Control

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Personalized and targeted ad effectiveness is greater when consumers have greater ability (or at least perceived) to control their privacy \citep{tucker2013}
\item
  Consumers' perceived information is the mediator through which self-protection, industry self-regulation, and government mandates reduce privacy concerns. \citep{xu2012research}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    But consumers can also disclose too much info, leaving them vulnerable, when they have greater perceived controls \citep{brandimarte2012economics}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Propositions:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  ``Firms that prioritize data privacy in an authentic way will experience positive performance''
\item
  ``Firms that involve their customers in the info privacy dialogue will experience positive performance''
\item
  ``Firms that implement privacy promoting practices will experiences positive performance under the condition that they align data privacy practices across all aspects of the firm''
\item
  ``Firms that focus on what they do right with respect to data privacy will experience positive performance''
\item
  ``Firms that commit to data privacy practices over the long-term will experience positive performance''
\item
  ``Firms that embody these privacy as strategy tenets will experience higher consumer trust.''
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{psychology-of-privacy}{%
\section{Psychology of Privacy}\label{psychology-of-privacy}}

\citep{brough2022} Consumers' response to privacy notices (bulletproof glass effect)

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Study 1: Managers expect a privacy notice will make customers feel more secure

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Since managers see that privacy notices as formal legal contract (i.e., binding agreements that dictate how a firm can collect, use and store data), they would expect that this formal contract-based approach can enhance consumers' comfort in purchasing a firm's product.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Studies 2, 3, 5: consistent with bulletproof glass increasing feelings of vulnerability (despite the protection offers), formal privacy notices can decrease consumer trust, and purchase interest (despite objective protection emphasis)

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    On the one hand, privacy is considered a social contract (Consumer perception of privacy invasion versus respect is governed by norm), and firms that respect these expectation can increase consumers' trust \citep{mccole2010trust} and increase purchase intention\citep{eastlick2006understanding}, and those that violate these norms will receive negative WOM \citep{miyazaki2009perceived}. Benefits for consumers would not negate this negative reactions \citep{kim2019seeing}. These social contracts can enhance trust \citep{kim2019seeing}
  \item
    On the other hand, formal contracts (instead of social contract) can undermine trust (similar to the bulletproof in unusual settings) \citep{malhotra2002effects}: Evidence from that multi-round trust game that consumers are less likely to trust when a formal contract was created in the first round than without the contract.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Study 4: when consumers had a priori that they should be distrustful, the unintended consequence of privacy notice did not materialize.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    When consumers do not have potential harm in mind, when seeing a bulletproof glass (i.e., in unexpected situations), they will react more negatively than when some potential harm is expected
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Study 5 and 6: when benevolence cues were added to privacy notices, the unintended consequence of privacy notice did not materialize

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    To increase trust, one can increase either benevolence or competence. Because benevolence-trust can induce consumers to view privacy notices as social contracts rather than formal contracts (as compared to using competence-trust).
  \item
    Since benevolence-trust is affective where as ability-trust is cognitive, we can use LIWC to score whether a privacy notice regarding its proportion of words that reflect affect process and proportion of words that reflect cognitive process
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Study 7: the presence and conspicuous absence of privacy info are enough too in decrease purchase intent.

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Use Apple's privacy nutrition labels to examine the presence and conspicuous absence of a privacy notice in terms of triggering decreased purchase interest.
  \item
    Apps were not required to include privacy notices (between 08/2017 and 05/2018), only half of the apps included a privacy policy link \citep{story2018apps}). In 12/2020, Apple mandated privacy labels in the App Store. Hence, \citep{brough2022} found that apps with a privacy notice conspicuously absence or present decease app downloads as compared to those without privacy notice.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}

Even though previous study posits that transparency regarding customer data can \textbf{reduce} perceived vulnerability \citep{martin2017data}, \citep{brough2022} posit that privacy notices can make costumers feel \textbf{more} vulnerable (similar to the bulletproof glass analogy)

The ``bulletproof glass effect'' is the increased purchase interest resulting from exposure to a privacy notice'' \citep[p.~740]{brough2022}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  When consumers notice that their data have been collected without consent, click-through rates decrease \citep{kim2019seeing, aguirre2015unraveling}
\item
  Consumers prefer to purchase from website with higher levels of privacy protection \citep{tsai2011effect}
\item
  Even though consumers were predicted to be rational in their response to privacy-related info, consumers are more malleable and less intuitive: Consumers are willing to tradeoff privacy in response to

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    architecture and framing \citep{adjerid2019choice, brandimarte2013misplaced}
  \item
    small inconveniences or incentives \citep{athey2017digital}
  \item
    greater perceived control over personal info \citep{mourey2020past, tucker2013}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\citep{martin2017data}: The impacts of a data breach on a company's performance are mitigated by the provision of transparency and control, which compensate for the vulnerabilities highlighted by consumers and mitigate the impact of a data breach on firm performance.

\citep{martin2016} The low likelihood of litigation paired with the backdrop of a data breach (a potentially rare event in some industries) suggests that businesses would continue to advocate modest consumer information privacy regulation, keeping the privacy management parts under their control.

disconnect between consumers' declared privacy desires and their actual privacy policies (even though people say that they are concerned about privacy, they still hare their sensitive personal information freely). \citep{martin2016}

\hypertarget{tradeoff}{%
\subsection{Tradeoff}\label{tradeoff}}

\citep{chellappa2005}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  This study examines the usage of online personalization after the tradeoff between personalization value and privacy concerns. More specifically, they found that value for personalization will increase the likelihood of using personalized services, but concern for privacy will decrease the likelihood of using personalized services.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Trust in vendor positively moderates the use of personalization. Hence, online vendors can leverage trust building activities to acquire and use customer info.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  This study provides support for orthogonality of personalization and privacy, vendors can independently develop personalized products and strategies to alleviate consumers' privacy concerns.
\item
  Personalization is defined as ``the ability to proactively tailor products and purchase experience to the tastes of individual consumers based upon their personal and preference information.'' (p.~181), which depends on

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Vendors' ability to acquire and process consumer info
  \item
    Consumers' willingness to share info and use personalized services.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Personalization can increase switching cost (filling out more information if one switches to another competitor) and loyalty \citep{alba1997interactive}. In the offline it is used to extract implicit price premiums, but in the online context, vendors are expected to do so (p.~183).

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Online personalization's main benefits are product or service fit and proactive delivery.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Privacy concerns:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    ``consumer is willing to share her preference information in exchange for apparent benefits, such as convenience, from using personalized products and services'' (p.~186). This is a type of social exchange where consumers expect that their expected (personalization) gain is greater than their (privacy) loss
  \item
    Privacy is defined as ``an individual's ability to control the terms by which their personal information is acquired and used.'' (p.~186)
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\citep{white2004consumer}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Although individuals with somewhat deep connection views were more likely to reveal ``privacy-related'' material, they were less likely to reveal humiliating information.
\item
  Although loyal customers found the exchange of privacy-related personal information for customized benefit offerings (relative to noncustomized offerings) attractive, the opposite was true for embarrassing information; these participants appeared to find the exchange of customized offerings for this type of information unattractive.
\end{itemize}

\citep{wattal2012}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Consumers respond favorably when businesses employ product-based personalisation (where the usage of information is not explicitly mentioned).
\item
  Consumers, on the other side, react unfavorably when businesses are explicit about how they use personally identifiable information (i.e., a personalized greeting).
\item
  consumer familiarity with businesses moderates consumers' unfavorable reactions to personalized greetings.
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{no-tradeoff}{%
\subsection{No tradeoff}\label{no-tradeoff}}

\citep{tucker2013} personalized ad and privacy controls in social networks

\begin{itemize}
\item
  found that personalized ad was ineffective before Facebook's introduction of privacy controls, but was twice as effective at attracting users after the shift in Facebook's policy (because they have more control over their personal info)
\item
  when sites can assure consumers that they are in control of their privacy, personalization can generate higher click-through rates.
\item
  DiD from Facebook introduction of more privacy controls for users.
\end{itemize}

\citep{walrave2016} personalization and privacy in social network ad

Contributions:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Even though this study hypothesize that a moderate level of personalization is optimal in ad effectiveness, they found the highest personalisation condition yielded the most positive response, and privacy concerns did not mitigate its impacts (authors justify that maybe persoanlization is not high enough to trigger the persuasion knowledge). In short, there is no tradeoff between personalization and privacy on brand engagement.
\end{itemize}

Definitions:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Personalization in the marketing communication context is defined as ``creating persuasive messages that refer to aspects of a person's self'' \citep{maslowska2011}
\item
  Evidence of positive impact of personalization on performance

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    on brand responses \citep{bauer2014}
  \item
    on campaign responses \citep{kim2012}
  \item
    traditional banner ad context, more positive persuasive effects \citep{tam2005web}
  \item
    email newsletters, more positive persuasive effects \citep{maslowska2011effectiveness}
  \item
    personalized mobile coupons are evaluated positively and more likely to be redeemed \citep{xu2008combining}
  \item
    Positive relationship with brand engagement \citep{chu2011viral}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  U-shaped impact of personalization on ad performance:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Positive: Personalization can evoke central information processing due to its high self-relevant \citep{cho2004people}. According to information processing theory, consumers are driven to elaborate on relevant messages, which increases attention, elaboration, and strong attitudes \citep{petty1986}. Hence, more personalization, more positive ad response.
  \item
    Negative: personalization increases skepticism toward ad due to the persuasion knowledge model \citep{friestad1994}. Knowing that a brand tries to persuade, one triggers persuasion knowledge which diminish persuasion effects. For example, people resist personalized emails when personal info is highly distintive \citep{white2008getting}

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      Consumers privacy concerns can enhance this negative relationship (i.e., reactance).
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Privacy is defined as a ``selective control of access to the self or to one's group'' \citep{altman1976conceptual}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    People want to strive a balance between openness and closeness (p.~604). When people feel their privacy concerns is threatened by personalization, they have coping strategies to protect their privacy from marketers \citep{youn2009determinants, grant2005young}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\citep{conitzer2012}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  A monopolist model with a continuum of heterogeneous consumers and the option for them to remain anonymous and avoid being recognized as prior customers, maybe at a cost.
\item
  When customers have the option to keep their anonymity, they all prefer to do so on an individual basis, which generates the most profit for the monopolist.
\item
  Consumers can gain from higher anonymity costs, but only up to a point when the effect turns against them.
\item
  It frequently harms consumers if the monopolist or an unaffiliated third party controls the cost of anonymity.
\end{itemize}

    Consumers did not uniformly increase data allowances and continued to restrict permissions for sensitive information.

\hypertarget{return-on-investment-roi}{%
\subsection{Return on Investment (ROI)}\label{return-on-investment-roi}}

\[
ROI = \frac{\text{Net Profit}}{\text{Investment}}
\]

Similarly, return on marketing investment

\[
ROIM = \frac{IRAM - CM}{MS}
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  IRAM = Incremental Revenue Attributable to Marketing
\item
  CM = Cost of the Marketing Investment
\item
  MS = Marketing Spending
\end{itemize}

If ROMI is positive, then firm is on doing well.

\hypertarget{economic-value-added}{%
\subsection{Economic Value Added}\label{economic-value-added}}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  also known as economic profit.
\item
  is a measure based on the residual wealth calculated by deducting its cost of capital from its operating profit, adjusted for taxes on a cash basis.
\item
  measures the value a company generates from its invested funds.
\item
  EVA relies heavily on invested capital. Hence, more suitable for asset-rich companies, whereas companies with intangible assets, such as technology businesses, may not be good candidates.
\end{itemize}

\[
EVA = NOPAT - (Invested Capital * WACC)
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\item
  NOPAT = Net Operating profit after taxes = Operating Profit x (1-Tax Rate)
\item
  Invested capital = Debt + capital leases + shareholders' equity = Equity + long-term debt at the beginning of the period
\item
  WACC = Weighted average cost of capital (average rate of return a company expects to pay its investors).

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    \(WACC = \frac{Ke \times E}{E+D} + \frac{Kd \times (1-t) \times D}{E +D }\)

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      Ke = required return on equity
    \item
      Kd(1-t) = after tax return on debt.
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  (WACC* capital invested) is also known as a \textbf{finance charge}
\end{itemize}

Invested capital can also be calculated as (Total Assets - Current Liabilities). Hence, the modified version of EVA is:

\[
EVA = NOPAT - (\text{total assets} - \text{current liabilities}) * WACC
\]

\hypertarget{market-value-added}{%
\subsection{Market Value Added}\label{market-value-added}}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  is the amount of wealth that a company is able to create for its stakeholders since its foundation.
\item
  (the current market value of the company's stock - the initial invested capital)
\end{itemize}

\[
MVA = \text{market value of shares (or enterprise value)} - \text{book value of shareholders' equity}
\]

Following Fama and French's \href{http://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/variable_definitions.html}{definition}:

``BE is the book value of stockholders' equity, plus balance sheet deferred taxes and investment tax credit (if available), minus the book value of preferred stock. Depending on availability, we use the redemption, liquidation, or par value (in that order) to estimate the book value of preferred stock. Stockholders' equity is the value reported by Moody's or Compustat, if it is available. If not, we measure stockholders' equity as the book value of common equity plus the par value of preferred stock, or the book value of assets minus total liabilities (in that order)'' (cite \citep{davis2000})

\hypertarget{capabilities}{%
\subsection{Capabilities}\label{capabilities}}

\citep{dutta1999} Marketing capability is critical for high-technology markets

Insights

\begin{itemize}
\item
  A company's sales are increased by a solid foundation of innovative technologies that positively affect consumers' perceptions of the benefits of its product's externalities.
\item
  For businesses with a strong technological foundation, marketing capability has the biggest impact on the production of innovation that has been quality-adjusted. The companies that stand to benefit the most from great marketing capabilities are those with a solid R\&D foundation.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    because a company may have tremendous R\&D capabilities but be unable to translate them into commercially viable items due to weak marketing skills
  \end{itemize}
\item
  The interaction of marketing and R\&D capabilities is the most significant factor in determining a firm's performance.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    High tech firm need to have both the ability to come up with innovation constantly and the ability to commercialize these innovations.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  A firm's capability is defined as ``its ability to deploy the resources (inputs) available to it to achieve the desired objective(s) (output).''

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Logically, \textbf{the higher the functional capability a firm has, the more efficiently it is able to deploy its productive inputs to achieve its functional objectives}.
  \item
    Equivalently, the lower the functional inefficiency, the higher the functional capability of the firm
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Operationalization

\textbf{Marketing Capability}

Sales = f(technological base, advertising stock, stock of marketing expenditure, investment in customer relationships, installed base)

Weight for marketing expenditure = 0.5 \citep[p.~281]{dutta2005}

Advertising stock weight = 0.4 \citep{peles1971} or 0.5 \citep{wang2017}

\textbf{R\&D Capability}

2 dimensions of the quality of technological output

\begin{itemize}
\item
  innovativeness \citep{trajtenberg1990, trajtenberg1990a}
\item
  width of applicability \citep{jaffe1993}
\end{itemize}

Quality-adjusted technological output = f(technological base, cumulative R\&D expenditure, marketing capability)

R\&D expenditure weight = 0.4 \citep[p.~281]{dutta2005}

\textbf{Operations Capability}

Cost of production = f(output, cost of capital, labor cost, technological base, marketing capability)

Replication

As the time of this writing, the US Patents by WRDS dataset only covers from 2011 to 2019. Hence, I can only replicate the results in this period but not the years in the study (1985 - 1994). Alternatively, you can visit \href{https://bulkdata.uspto.gov/}{USPTO} to download the raw dataset and create your own matching algorithm based on company names.
