Innovativeness-adjusted technological output:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Calculate the average number of citations receive by all patents belonging the firms in the sample within one industry (defined by sic1, sic2, sic3, sic4)
\item
  The weight assigned to a firm's patents = \# of citations / industry sample average
\item
  Tech\_innv = sum of citation-weighted patents within a firm in a year.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# calculate industry average citation based on}
\CommentTok{\# sic1}
\NormalTok{tech\_innv1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{aggregate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ tech\_innv}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{citation\_count,}
                   \AttributeTok{by =} \FunctionTok{list}\NormalTok{(tech\_innv}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{sic1),}
                   \AttributeTok{FUN =}\NormalTok{ mean) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{rename}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{sic1 =} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,}
           \AttributeTok{mean\_cite\_ind1 =} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# sic2}
\NormalTok{tech\_innv2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{aggregate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ tech\_innv}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{citation\_count,}
                   \AttributeTok{by =} \FunctionTok{list}\NormalTok{(tech\_innv}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{sic2),}
                   \AttributeTok{FUN =}\NormalTok{ mean) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{rename}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{sic2 =} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,}
           \AttributeTok{mean\_cite\_ind2 =} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# sic3}
\NormalTok{tech\_innv3 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{aggregate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ tech\_innv}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{citation\_count,}
                   \AttributeTok{by =} \FunctionTok{list}\NormalTok{(tech\_innv}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{sic3),}
                   \AttributeTok{FUN =}\NormalTok{ mean) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{rename}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{sic3 =} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,}
           \AttributeTok{mean\_cite\_ind3 =} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# sic4}
\NormalTok{tech\_innv4 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{aggregate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ tech\_innv}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{citation\_count,}
                   \AttributeTok{by =} \FunctionTok{list}\NormalTok{(tech\_innv}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{sic),}
                   \AttributeTok{FUN =}\NormalTok{ mean) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{rename}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{sic =} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,}
           \AttributeTok{mean\_cite\_ind4 =} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# merge all four sic types together}
\NormalTok{tech\_innv\_sic }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ tech\_innv4 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}
        \AttributeTok{sic3 =} \FunctionTok{substr}\NormalTok{(sic, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
        \AttributeTok{sic2 =} \FunctionTok{substr}\NormalTok{(sic, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{),}
        \AttributeTok{sic1 =} \FunctionTok{substr}\NormalTok{(sic, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    ) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{full\_join}\NormalTok{(tech\_innv3, }\AttributeTok{by =} \StringTok{"sic3"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{full\_join}\NormalTok{(tech\_innv2, }\AttributeTok{by =} \StringTok{"sic2"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{full\_join}\NormalTok{(tech\_innv1, }\AttributeTok{by =} \StringTok{"sic1"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    
    \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(sic1, sic2, sic3))}

\CommentTok{\# note that a modification from Dutta\textquotesingle{}s paper is that I use the average number of citations received by all the patents belonging the firms in the sample within one industry (because industry average citations might differ)}
\CommentTok{\# Dutta\textquotesingle{}s paper did not do this because they consider only one industry }

\CommentTok{\# calculate the Tech\_innv}
\NormalTok{tech\_innv }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ wrdsapps\_patents\_link }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(gvkey, patnum, sic) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    
    \FunctionTok{inner\_join}\NormalTok{(wrdsapps\_patents\_citations\_by\_year, }\AttributeTok{by =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"patnum"} \OtherTok{=} \StringTok{"cited\_patnum"}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    
    \CommentTok{\# match with the firm and year data }
    \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(gvkey }\SpecialCharTok{\%in\%}\NormalTok{ capability}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{gvkey) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    
    \FunctionTok{inner\_join}\NormalTok{(tech\_innv\_sic, }\AttributeTok{by =} \StringTok{"sic"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    
    \CommentTok{\# create the weight assigned to a firm\textquotesingle{}s patent}
    \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{weight1 =}\NormalTok{ citation\_count }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ mean\_cite\_ind1, }
           \AttributeTok{weight2 =}\NormalTok{ citation\_count }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ mean\_cite\_ind2,}
           \AttributeTok{weight3 =}\NormalTok{ citation\_count }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ mean\_cite\_ind3,}
           \AttributeTok{weight4 =}\NormalTok{ citation\_count }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ mean\_cite\_ind4) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    
    \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(gvkey, grantyear) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \CommentTok{\# create the citation{-}weighted patent count}
    \FunctionTok{summarize}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{tech\_innv1 =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(weight1), }
              \AttributeTok{tech\_innv2 =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(weight2),}
              \AttributeTok{tech\_innv3 =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(weight3),}
              \AttributeTok{tech\_innv4 =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(weight4)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{()}

\FunctionTok{rm}\NormalTok{(tech\_innv\_sic,}
\NormalTok{   tech\_innv1,}
\NormalTok{   tech\_innv2,}
\NormalTok{   tech\_innv3,}
\NormalTok{   tech\_innv4)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Width-of-applicability-technological output 1. Calculate the proportion of citations received by a patent from firms belonging outside of focal SIC code (sic1, sic2, sic3, sic4) = \# of citations received by a patent from firms outside the focal SIC code / the total number of citation the patent received. 2. The weight assigned to a firm's patent = the proportion of outside citations for the patent/ the industry sample average proportion 3. Tech\_width = The sum of the ``proportion-of-outside citation''-weighted patent in a year for a firm

    \FunctionTok{rename}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{n\_sim1 =}\NormalTok{ n)}

\CommentTok{\# sic2}
\NormalTok{outside\_citation\_sic2 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ wrdsapps\_patents\_citations\_out\_ind }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(cited\_patnum, cited\_pat\_gyear, sim2) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{count}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \CommentTok{\# get only citations outside of the patent\textquotesingle{}s industry}
    \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(sim2 }\SpecialCharTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(sim2)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{rename}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{n\_sim2 =}\NormalTok{ n)}

\CommentTok{\# sic3}
\NormalTok{outside\_citation\_sic3 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ wrdsapps\_patents\_citations\_out\_ind }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(cited\_patnum, cited\_pat\_gyear, sim3) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{count}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \CommentTok{\# get only citations outside of the patent\textquotesingle{}s industry}
    \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(sim3 }\SpecialCharTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(sim3)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{rename}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{n\_sim3 =}\NormalTok{ n)}

\CommentTok{\# sic4}
\NormalTok{outside\_citation\_sic4 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ wrdsapps\_patents\_citations\_out\_ind }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(cited\_patnum, cited\_pat\_gyear, sim4) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{count}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \CommentTok{\# get only citations outside of the patent\textquotesingle{}s industry}
    \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(sim4 }\SpecialCharTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(sim4)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{rename}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{n\_sim4 =}\NormalTok{ n)}


\NormalTok{tech\_width }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ total\_citation }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    
    \FunctionTok{full\_join}\NormalTok{(outside\_citation\_sic1, }\AttributeTok{by =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"cited\_patnum"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cited\_pat\_gyear"}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{full\_join}\NormalTok{(outside\_citation\_sic2, }\AttributeTok{by =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"cited\_patnum"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cited\_pat\_gyear"}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{full\_join}\NormalTok{(outside\_citation\_sic3, }\AttributeTok{by =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"cited\_patnum"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cited\_pat\_gyear"}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{full\_join}\NormalTok{(outside\_citation\_sic4, }\AttributeTok{by =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"cited\_patnum"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cited\_pat\_gyear"}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    
    
    \CommentTok{\# fill in 0 (those patents without any citations outside of their industry)}
    \FunctionTok{replace}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{is.na}\NormalTok{(.), }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    
    \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{weight1 =}\NormalTok{ n\_sim1 }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ n,}
           \AttributeTok{weight2 =}\NormalTok{ n\_sim2 }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ n,}
           \AttributeTok{weight3 =}\NormalTok{ n\_sim3 }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ n,}
           \AttributeTok{weight4 =}\NormalTok{ n\_sim4 }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ n) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    
    \CommentTok{\# get company gvkey for each patent}
    \FunctionTok{inner\_join}\NormalTok{(wrdsapps\_patents\_link }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                   \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(gvkey, patnum, sic),}
               \AttributeTok{by =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"cited\_patnum"} \OtherTok{=} \StringTok{"patnum"}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    
    \CommentTok{\# step 3: get proportion{-}of{-}outside citation{-}weighted patent}
    \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(gvkey, cited\_pat\_gyear) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{summarize}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{tech\_width1 =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(weight1),}
              \AttributeTok{tech\_width2 =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(weight2),}
              \AttributeTok{tech\_width3 =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(weight3),}
              \AttributeTok{tech\_width4 =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(weight4)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
    \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{()}


\FunctionTok{rm}\NormalTok{(outside\_citation\_sic1,}
\NormalTok{   outside\_citation\_sic2,}
\NormalTok{   outside\_citation\_sic3,}
\NormalTok{   outside\_citation\_sic4,}
\NormalTok{   total\_citation)}

\hypertarget{wrds}{%
\section{WRDS}\label{wrds}}

Retrieve data from WRDS

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# to set up connection from R to WRDS (https://wrds{-}www.wharton.upenn.edu/pages/support/programming{-}wrds/programming{-}r/r{-}from{-}your{-}computer/)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(RPostgres)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(dplyr)}

\CommentTok{\# I\textquotesingle{}ve set up wrds connection before hand. Please use your username and password here.}

\CommentTok{\# wrds \textless{}{-} dbConnect(Postgres(),}
\CommentTok{\#                   host=\textquotesingle{}wrds{-}pgdata.wharton.upenn.edu\textquotesingle{},}
\CommentTok{\#                   port=9737,}
\CommentTok{\#                   dbname=\textquotesingle{}wrds\textquotesingle{},}
\CommentTok{\#                   sslmode=\textquotesingle{}require\textquotesingle{},}
\CommentTok{\#                   user=\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{})}

\CommentTok{\# Check variables (column headers) in COMP ANNUAL FUNDAMENTAL}
\CommentTok{\#uses the already{-}established wrds connection to prepare the SQL query string and save the query as the result res.}
\CommentTok{\# check avaiable databases: https://wrds{-}web.wharton.upenn.edu/wrds/tools/variable.cfm?vendor\_id=7}
\NormalTok{res }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{dbSendQuery}\NormalTok{(wrds, }\StringTok{"select column\_name}
\StringTok{                   from information\_schema.columns}
\StringTok{                   where table\_schema=\textquotesingle{}compa\textquotesingle{}}
\StringTok{                   and table\_name=\textquotesingle{}funda\textquotesingle{}}
\StringTok{                   order by column\_name"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{data }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{dbFetch}\NormalTok{(res, }\AttributeTok{n=}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\CommentTok{\# fetches the data that results from running the query res against wrds and stores it as data}
\FunctionTok{dbClearResult}\NormalTok{(res) }\CommentTok{\# closes the connection}
\FunctionTok{head}\NormalTok{(data)}

\CommentTok{\# select everything}
\NormalTok{res }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{dbSendQuery}\NormalTok{(wrds, }\StringTok{"select * from compa.funda"}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# from compa.funda}

\CommentTok{\# only select the following variables}
\NormalTok{res }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{dbSendQuery}\NormalTok{(wrds, }\StringTok{"select gvkey, datadate, fyear, indfmt, consol, popsrc, datafmt, tic, cusip, conm, curcd, fyr, act, at, bkvlps, ceq, ch, che, dltt, dlc, emp, np, exchg, cik, costat, naicsh,mkvalt from compa.funda"}\NormalTok{) }\CommentTok{\#check variables from (https://wrds{-}web.wharton.upenn.edu/wrds/ds/comp/funda/index.cfm?navId=80)}

\CommentTok{\# res \textless{}{-} dbSendQuery(wrds, "select gvkey, gp from compa.funda") \#check variables from}
\NormalTok{data1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{dbFetch}\NormalTok{(res, }\AttributeTok{n=}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\FunctionTok{dbClearResult}\NormalTok{(res)}

\NormalTok{data }\OtherTok{=}\NormalTok{ data1 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{distinct}\NormalTok{(gvkey,datadate,fyear,tic,conm,}\AttributeTok{.keep\_all =}\NormalTok{ T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

    \CommentTok{\#store your ids}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# {-}*{-} coding: utf{-}8 {-}*{-}}

\CommentTok{\# Sample Python code for youtube.search.list}
\CommentTok{\# See instructions for running these code samples locally:}

\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ os}

\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ google\_auth\_oauthlib.flow}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ googleapiclient.discovery}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ googleapiclient.errors}

\NormalTok{scopes }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube.force{-}ssl"}\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ main():}
    \CommentTok{\# Disable OAuthlib\textquotesingle{}s HTTPS verification when running locally.}
    \CommentTok{\# *DO NOT* leave this option enabled in production.}
\NormalTok{    os.environ[}\StringTok{"OAUTHLIB\_INSECURE\_TRANSPORT"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"1"}

\NormalTok{    api\_service\_name }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"youtube"}
\NormalTok{    api\_version }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"v3"}
\NormalTok{    client\_secrets\_file }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"YOUR\_CLIENT\_SECRET\_FILE.json"}

    \CommentTok{\# Get credentials and create an API client}
\NormalTok{    flow }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ google\_auth\_oauthlib.flow.InstalledAppFlow.from\_client\_secrets\_file(}
\NormalTok{        client\_secrets\_file, scopes)}
\NormalTok{    credentials }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ flow.run\_console()}
\NormalTok{    youtube }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ googleapiclient.discovery.build(}
\NormalTok{        api\_service\_name, api\_version, credentials}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{credentials)}

\NormalTok{    request }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ youtube.search().}\BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}
\NormalTok{        part}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"snippet"}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{        maxResults}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{25}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{        q}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"surfing"}
\NormalTok{    )}
\NormalTok{    response }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ request.execute()}

    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(response)}

\ControlFlowTok{if} \VariableTok{\_\_name\_\_} \OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"\_\_main\_\_"}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{    main()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Another way, but this is a dirty crawler, not for production

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ re, urllib}
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ random }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ randint}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ random\_str(str\_size):}
\NormalTok{    res }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{""}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{xrange}\NormalTok{(str\_size):}
\NormalTok{        x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ randint(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{25}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{        c }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{chr}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{ord}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}a\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{x)}
\NormalTok{        res }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ c}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ res}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ find\_watch(text,pos):}
\NormalTok{    start }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ text.find(}\StringTok{"watch?v="}\NormalTok{,pos)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ (start}\OperatorTok{\textless{}}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{):}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{,}\VariableTok{None}
\NormalTok{    end }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ text.find(}\StringTok{" "}\NormalTok{,start)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ (end}\OperatorTok{\textless{}}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{):}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{,}\VariableTok{None}

    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ (end}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{start }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{200}\NormalTok{): }\CommentTok{\#silly heuristics, probably not a must}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{,}\VariableTok{None}

    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ text[start:end}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], start}


\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ find\_instance\_links():}
\NormalTok{    base\_url }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}https://www.youtube.com/results?search\_query=\textquotesingle{}}
\NormalTok{    url }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ base\_url}\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{random\_str(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
    \CommentTok{\#print url}

\NormalTok{    r }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ urllib.urlopen(url).read()}

\NormalTok{    links }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{\}}

\NormalTok{    pos }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{0}
    \ControlFlowTok{while} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        link,pos }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{  find\_watch(r,pos)}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ link }\OperatorTok{==} \VariableTok{None} \KeywordTok{or}\NormalTok{ pos }\OperatorTok{==} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{:}
            \ControlFlowTok{break}
\NormalTok{        pos }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}
        \CommentTok{\#print link}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ (}\StringTok{";"} \KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ link):}
            \ControlFlowTok{continue}
\NormalTok{        links[link] }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1}

\NormalTok{    items\_list }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ links.items()}

\NormalTok{    list\_size }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(items\_list)}
\NormalTok{    selected }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ randint(list\_size}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{,list\_size}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ items\_list[selected][}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}


\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{xrange}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    sleep(randint(}\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{)) }\CommentTok{\# pause randomly between 7 and 20 seconds}
\NormalTok{    link }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ find\_instance\_links()}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{ link}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\hypertarget{consumer-expenditure}{%
\section{Consumer Expenditure}\label{consumer-expenditure}}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  A consumer unit: ``a single person, or group of person who live together and who share responsibilities for most major expenditures.''
\item
  The ``Reference Person'' is \textbf{the first person named} when the respondent is asked, ``Who is responsible for owning or renting this home?''
\item
  2 components to the Consumer Expenditure:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Interview survey

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      for ``big ticket'' and recurring expenditures, and global estimates on others
    \item
      every three months for four quarter
    \item
      rotating-panel survey
    \item
      6,000 consumer units each quarter
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Diary survey

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      small-ticket, frequently purchased items
    \item
      independent from the interview survey
    \item
      about 14,000 diaries within families each year
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Table format

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    annual

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Jan to Dec: since 1984
    \item
      July to June: since 2013
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    two-year (Jan year 1 - Dec year 2)

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      since 1986
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Experimental research

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    all consumer units (available on request)
  \item
    E.g., income tables, generational groups (e.g., millennial, gen X)
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

  \texttt{https://agify.io/}
\item
  \texttt{https://nationalize.io/}
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{google-trends}{%
\section{Google Trends}\label{google-trends}}

Online search volume and news reporting show a strong correlation, while academic publishing lag behind online public interest due to its delayed review and publication process \citep{nghiem2016}. This result was interpreted as news serves as a conductor between the research and the public community.

Google Trends only return

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Data Granularity & Data Window \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Hourly Data & Last 7 days \\
Daily Data & Less than 9 months \\
Weekly Data & between 9 months and 5 years \\
Monthly Data & Longer than 5 years \\
\end{longtable}

Since the data is indexed for the chosen time window, for the same keywords with different time windows might result in different index values.

\subsection{Relative Search}\label{relative-search}}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Scaling method (overlapping method) (recommended)
\end{enumerate}

A way to get daily data from \texttt{gtrendsR} readily is proposed by \href{http://alexdyachenko.com/all/how-to-get-daily-google-trends-data-for-any-period-with-r/}{Alex Dyachenko}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Get daily estimates for the window less than 9 months
\item
  Get monthly estimates for your desired time frame
\item
  Multiply daily estimates for each month from step 1 by their weights from step 2
\item
  Concatenation method (normalization/\href{https://github.com/GeneralMills/pytrends/blob/master/pytrends/dailydata.py}{dailydata} method)
\end{enumerate}

Daily data are concatenated from 1-month queries and normalized by weekly trends data, which has been done in this \href{https://medium.com/@bewerunge.franz/google-trends-how-to-acquire-daily-data-for-broad-time-frames-b6c6dfe200e6}{post}

From this \href{https://towardsdatascience.com/reconstruct-google-trends-daily-data-for-extended-period-75b6ca1d3420}{post}, we can be sure that the scaling method is better than the normalization method

Rate limit:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  1,400 requests in 4 hours
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(gtrendsR)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(tidyverse)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(lubridate)}

\NormalTok{get\_daily\_gtrend }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}
    \ControlFlowTok{function}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{keyword =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}7eleven\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}3M\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{),}
             \AttributeTok{geo =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}US\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}
             \AttributeTok{from =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}2013{-}01{-}01\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}
             \AttributeTok{to =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}2013{-}02{-}15\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{) \{}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ (}\FunctionTok{ymd}\NormalTok{(to) }\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}=} \FunctionTok{floor\_date}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{Sys.Date}\NormalTok{(), }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}month\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)) \{}

\hypertarget{definitions}{%
\section{Definitions}\label{definitions}}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Structural in quantitative marketing: An estimation strategy where we assume and impose a structure to the consumer's maximization problem and these parameters are of the consumers' utility functions \citep{erdem1996a}.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    These parameter are policy-invariant.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Reduced form brand choice model: functions of marketing strategy variables (e..g, marketing mix). Hence, reduced-form models' parameters are variant to policy. So it's hard to study outcome of policy implementation may be reliable.
\end{itemize}

Uncertainty about product characteristics + learning behavior affect brand choice.

Two models (good in cases where consumer learning is vital to the choice process):

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Dynamic structural model with immediate utility maximization
\item
  Forward-looking dynamic structural model (i.e., consumers don't choose products based on their current utility, but also future utility).
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{analytical-models}{%
\chapter{Analytical Models}\label{analytical-models}}

Marketing models consists of

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Analytical Model: pure mathematical-based research
\item
  Empirical Model: data analysis.
\end{enumerate}

``A model is a representation of the most important elements of a perceived real-world system''.

Marketing model improves decision-making

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Econometric models

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Description
  \item
    Prediction
  \item
    Simulation
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Optimization models

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    maximize profit using market response model, cost functions, or any constraints.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Quasi- and Field experimental analyses
\item
  Conjoint Choice Experiments.
\end{itemize}

``A decision calculus will be defined as a model-based set of procedures for processing data and judgments to assist a manager in his decision making''\citep{Little_1976}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  simple
\item
  robust
\item
  easy to control
\item
  adaptive
\item
  as complete as possible
\item
  easy to communicate with
\end{itemize}

\citep{moorthy1993}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Mathematical Theoretical Models
\item
  Logical Experimentation
\item
  An environment as a model, specified by assumptions

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Math assumptions for tractability
  \item
    Substantive assumptions for empirical testing
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Decision support modeling describe how things work, and theoretical modeling present how things should work.
\item
  Compensation package including salaries and commission is a tradeoff between reduced income risk and motivation to work hard.
\item
  Internal and External Validity are questions related to the boundaries conditions of your experiments.
\item
  ``Theories are tested by their predictions, not by the realism of their super model assumptions.'' (Friedman, 1953)
\end{itemize}

\citep{mcafee1996}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Competition is performed under uncertainty
\item
  Competition reveals hidden information

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Independent-private-values case: selling price = second highest valuation
  \item
    It's always better for sellers to reveal information since it reduces chances of cautious bidding that is resulted from the winner's curse
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Competition is better than bargaining

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Competition requires less computation and commitment abilities
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Competition creates effort incentives
\end{itemize}

\citep{leeflang2000}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Types of model:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Predictive model

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Sales model: using time series data
    \item
      Trial rate: using exponential growth.
    \item
      Product growth model: \citet{Bass_1969}
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Descriptive model

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Purchase incidence and purchase timing : use Poisson process
    \item
      Brand choice: Markov models or learning models.
    \item
      Pricing decisions in an oligopolistic market \citet{howard1968}
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Normative model

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      Profit maximization based on price, adverting and quality \citep{dorfman1976}, extended by \citep{roberts1964, lambin1970a}
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Later, \citet{Little_1970} introduced decision calculus and then multinomial logit model \citep{guadagni1983}

Potential marketing decision automation:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Promotion or pricing programs
\item
  Media allocation
\item
  Distribution
\item
  Product assortment
\item
  Direct mail solicitation
\end{itemize}

\citep{moorthy1985}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Definitions:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Rationality = maximizing subjective expected utility
  \item
    Intelligence = recognizing other firms are rational.
  \item
    Rules of the game include

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      \# of firms
    \item
      feasible set of actions
    \item
      utilities for each combination of moves
    \item
      sequence of moves
    \item
      the structure of info (who knows what and when?)
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Incomplete info stems from

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      unknown motivations
    \item
      unknown ability (capabilities)
    \item
      different knowledge of the world.
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Pure strategy = plan of action
  \item
    A mixed strategy = probability dist of pure strategies.
  \item
    Strategic form representation = sets of possible strategies for every firm and its payoffs.
  \item
    Equilibrium = a list of strategies in which ``no firm would like unilaterally to change its strategy.''
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Equilibrium is not outcome of a dynamic process.
\item
  Equilibrium Application

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Oligopolistic Competition

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Cournot (1838): quantities supplied: Cournot equilibrium. Changing quantities is more costly than changing prices
    \item
      Bertrand (1883): Bertrand equilibrium: pricing.
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Perfect competition
  \item
    Product Competition: Hotelling (1929): Principle of Minimum Differentiation is invalid.
  \item
    Entry:

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      first mover advantage
    \item
      deterrent strategy
    \item
      optimal for entrants or incumbents
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Channels
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Perfectness of equilibria

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Subgame perfectness
  \item
    Sequential rationality
  \item
    Trembling-hand perfectness
  \item
    Application

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Product and price competition in Oligopolies
    \item
      Strategic Entry Deterrence
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Dynamic games

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Long-term competition in oligopolies
  \item
    Implicit Collusion in practice : price match from leader firms
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Incomplete Information

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Durable goods pricing by a monopolist
  \item
    predatory pricing and limit pricing
  \item
    reputation, product quality, and prices
  \item
    Competitive bidding and auctions
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{building-an-analytical-model}{%
\section{Building An Analytical Model}\label{building-an-analytical-model}}

Notes by professor Sajeesh Sajeesh

Step 1: Get ``good'' idea (either from literature or industry)

Step 2: Assess the feasibility of the idea

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Is it interesting?
\item
  Can you tell a story?
\item
  Who is the target audience?
\item
  Opportunity cost
\end{itemize}

Step 3: Don't look at the literature too soon

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Even when you have an identical model as in the literature, it's ok (it allows you to think)
\end{itemize}

Step 4: BUild the model

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Simplest model first: 1 period, 2 product , linear utility function for consumers
\item
  Write down the model formulation
\item
  Everything should be as simple as possible .. but no simpler
\end{itemize}

Step 5: Generalizing the model

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Adding complexity
\end{itemize}

Step 6: Searching the literature

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If you find a paper, you can ask yourself why you didn't do what the author has done.
\end{itemize}

Step 7: Give a talk /seminar

Step 8: Write the paper

\hypertarget{hotelling-model}{%
\section{Hotelling Model}\label{hotelling-model}}

\citep{kim2006}: A location model with preference variety

\citep{hotelling1929}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Stability in competition
\item
  Duopoly is inherently unstable
\item
  Bertrand disagrees with Cournot, and Edgeworth elaborates on it.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    because Cournot's assumption of absolutely identical products between firms.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

seller try to \(p_2 < p_1 c(l-a-b)\)

the point of indifference

\[
p_1 + cx = p_2 + cy
\]

\begin{itemize}
\item
  c = cost per unit of time in each unit of line length
\item
  p = price
\item
  q = quantity
\item
  x, y = length from A and B respectively
\end{itemize}

\[
a + x + y + b = l
\]

is the length of the street

Hence, we have

\[
x = 0.5(l - a - b + \frac{p_2- p_1}{c}) \\
y = 0.5(l - a - b + \frac{p_1- p_2}{c})
\]

Profits will be

\[
\pi_1 = p_1 q_1 = p_1 (a+ x) = 0.5 (l + a - b) p_1 - \frac{p_1^2}{2c} + \frac{p_1 p_2}{2c} \\
\pi_2 = p_2 q_2 = p_2 (b+ y) = 0.5 (l + a - b) p_2 - \frac{p_2^2}{2c} + \frac{p_1 p_2}{2c}
\]

To set the price to maximize profit, we have

\[
\frac{\partial \pi_1}{\partial p_1} = 0.5 (l + a - b) - \frac{p_1}{c} + \frac{p_2}{2c} = 0 \\
\frac{\partial \pi_2}{\partial p_2} = 0.5 (l - a + b) - \frac{p_2}{c} + \frac{p_1}{2c} = 0
\]

which equals

\[
p_1 = c(l + \frac{a-b}{3}) \\
p_2 = c(l - \frac{a-b}{3})
\]

and

\[
q_1 = a + x = 0.5 (l + \frac{a -b}{3}) \\
q_2 = b + y = 0.5 (l - \frac{a-b}{3})
\]

with the SOC satisfied

In case of deciding locations, socialism works better than capitalism

\citep{daspremont1979}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Principle of Minimum Differentiation is invalid
\end{itemize}

\[
\pi_1 (p_1, p_2) = 
\begin{cases}
ap_1 + 0.5(l-a-b) p_1 + \frac{1}{2c}p_1 p_2 - \frac{1}{2c}p_1^2 & \text{if } |p_1 - p_2| \le c(l-a-b) \\
lp_1 & \text{if } p_1 < p_2 - c(l-a-b) \\
0 & \text{if } p_1 > p_2 + c(l-a-b)
\end{cases}
\]

and

\[
\pi_2 (p_1, p_2) = 
\begin{cases}
bp_2 + 0.5(l-a-b) p_2 + \frac{1}{2c}p_1 p_2  - \frac{1}{2c}p_2^2& \text{if } |p_1 - p_2| \le c(l-a-b) \\
lp_2 & \text{if } p_2 < p_1 - c(l-a-b) \\
0 & \text{if } p_2 > p_1 + c(l-a-b)
\end{cases}
\]

\hypertarget{positioning-models}{%
\section{Positioning Models}\label{positioning-models}}

\citet{tabuchi1995}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Relax Hotelling's model's assumption of uniform distribution of consumers to non-uniform distribution.
\item
  Assumptions:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Equal cost
  \item
    Consumers distributed over {[}0,1{]}
  \item
    \(F(x)\) = cumulative distribution of consumers where \(F(1) = 1\) = total population
  \item
    2 distributions:

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Traditional uniform density: \(f(x) =1\)
    \item
      New: triangular density: \(f(x) = 2 - 2|2x-1|\) which represents consumer concentration
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Transportation cost = quadratic function of distance.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Hence, marginal consumer is

\[
\bar{x} = (p_2 - p_1 + x^2_2-x_1^2)/2(x_2-x_1)
\]

then when \(x_1 < x_2\) the profit function is

\[
\Pi_1 = p_1 F(\bar{x})
\]

and

\[
\Pi_2 = p_2[1-F(\bar{x})]
\]

and vice versa for \(x_1 >x_2\), and Bertrand game when \(x_1 = x_2\)

\begin{itemize}
\item
  If firms pick \textbf{simultaneously} their locations, and then \textbf{simultaneously} their prices, and consumer density function is log-concave, then there is a unique Nash price equilibrium

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Under \textbf{uniform} distribution, firms choose to locate as far apart as possible (could be true when observing shopping centers are far away from cities), but then consumers have to buy products that are far away from their ideal.
  \item
    Under \textbf{triangular} density, no symmetric location can be found, but two asymmetric Nash location equilibrium can still be possible (decrease in equilibrium profits of both firms)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  If firms pick \textbf{sequentially} their locations, and pick their prices \textbf{simultaneously,}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Under both uniform and triangular, first entrant will locate at the market center
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{cournot---simultaneous-games}{%
\subsection{Cournot - Simultaneous Games}\label{cournot---simultaneous-games}}

\[
TC_i = c_i q_i \text{ where } i= 1,2 \\
P(Q) = a - bQ \\
Q = q_1 +q_2 \\
\pi_1 = \text{price} \times \text{quantity} - \text{cost} = [a - b(q_1 +q_2)]q_1 - c_1 q_1 \\
\pi_2 = \text{price} \times \text{quantity} - \text{cost} = [a - b(q_1 +q_2)]q_1 - c_2 q_2 \\
\]

\begin{equation} 
\frac{d \pi_1}{d q_1} = a - 2bq_1 - bq_2-c_1 = 0 (1)
\label{eq:cournot1}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\frac{d \pi_2}{d q_2} = a - 2bq_2 - bq_1-c_2 = 0 
\label{eq:cournot2}
\end{equation}

From \eqref{eq:cournot1}

\begin{equation}
q_1 = \frac{a-c_1}{2b} - \frac{q_2}{2} = R_1 (q_2)
\label{eq:cournot3}
\end{equation}

is called reaction function, for best response function

From \eqref{eq:cournot2}

\begin{equation}
q_2 = \frac{a-c_2}{2b} - \frac{q_1}{2} =
\label{eq:cournot4}
\end{equation}

\[
q_1 = \frac{a-c_1}{2b} - \frac{a-c_2}{4b} + \frac{q_1}{4}
\]

Hence,

\[
q_1^* = \frac{a-2c_1+ c_2}{3b} \\
q_2^* = \frac{a-2c_2 + c_1}{3b}
\]

Total quantity is

\[
Q = q_1 + q_2 = \frac{2a-c_1 -c_2}{3b}
\]

Price

\[
a-bQ = \frac{a+c_1+c_2}{3b}
\]

\hypertarget{stackelberg---sequential-games}{%
\subsection{Stackelberg - Sequential games}\label{stackelberg---sequential-games}}

also known as leader-follower games

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Stage 1: Firm 1 chooses quantity
\item
  Stage 2: Firm 2 chooses quantity
\end{itemize}

\[
c_2 = c_1 = c
\]

Stage 2: reaction function of firm 2 given quantity firm 1

\[
R_2(q_1) = \frac{a-c}{2b} - \frac{q_1}{2}
\]

Stage 1:

\[
\pi_1 = [a-b(q_1 + \frac{a-c}{2b} - \frac{q_1}{2})]q_1 - cq_1 \\
= [a-b( \frac{a-c}{2b} + \frac{q_1}{2}]q_1 + cq_1
\]

\[
\frac{d \pi_1}{d q_1} = 0
\]

Hence,

\[
\frac{a+c}{2} - b q_1 -c =0
\]

The Stackelberg equilibrium is

\[
q_1^* = \frac{a-c}{2b} \\
q_2^* = \frac{a-c}{4b}
\]

Under same price (c), Cournot =

\[
q_1 = q_2 = \frac{a-c}{3b}
\]

Leader produces more whereas the follower produces less compared to Cournot

\[
\frac{d \pi_W^*}{d \beta} <0
\]

for the entire quantity range \(d < \bar{d}\)

As \(\beta\) increases in \(\pi_W^*\) Firm W wants to reduce \(\beta\).

Low \(\beta\) wants more independent

Firms W want more differentiated product

On the other hand,

\[
\frac{d \pi_S^*}{d \beta} <0
\]

for a range of \(d < \bar{d}\)

Firm S profit increases as \(\beta\) decreases when d is small

Firm S profit increases as \(\beta\) increases when d is large

Firm S profit increases as as product are more substitute when d is large

Firm S profit increases as products are less differentiated when d is large

Snob:

\[
U_A = V - p_A - \theta t_s - \lambda_s(n_A) \\
U_B = V - p_B - (1-\theta) t_s - \lambda_s(n_B)
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(\lambda_s\) = sensitivity towards externality.
\item
  \(\theta\) is the position in the Hotelling's framework.
\item
  \(t_s\) is transportation cost.
\end{itemize}

Conformist

\[
U_A = V - p_A - \theta t_s + \lambda_c(n_A) \\
U_B = V - p_B - (1-\theta) t_s + \lambda_c(n_B)
\]

Rational Expectations Equilibrium

If your expectations are rational, then your expectation will be realized in equilibrium

Say, Marginal Snob = \(\theta_s\) and \(\beta\) = number of snob in the market

Snobs

\[
U_A^c \equiv U_B^c = \theta_s
\]

Conformists

\[
U_A^c =U_B^c = \theta_c
\]

Then, according to rational expectations equilibrium, we have

\[
\beta \theta_s +( 1- \beta) \theta_c = n_A \\
\beta (1-\theta_s) +( 1- \beta) (1-\theta_c) = n_B
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(\beta \theta_s\) = Number of snobs who buy from firm A
\item
  \((1-\beta)\theta_c\) = Number of conformists who buy from firm B
\item
  \(\beta(1-\theta_s)\) = Number of snobs who buy from firm B
\item
  \((1-\beta)(1-\theta_c)\) = Number of conformists who buy from firm B
\end{itemize}

which is the rational expectations equilibrium (whatever we expect happens in reality).

In other words, expectation are realized in equilibrium.

The number of people expected to buy the product is endogenous in the model, which will be the actual number of people who will buy it in the market.

We should not think of the expected value here in the same sense as expected value in empirical research (\(E(.)\)) because the expected value here is without any errors (specifically, measurement error).

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The utility function for snobs is such that overall when price increase for one product, snob will like to buy the product more. When price increases, conformist will reduce the purchase.
\end{itemize}

\section{Market Response Model}\label{market-response-model}}

Marketing Inputs:

\tightlist
\item
  Selling effort
\item
  advertising spending
\item

\end{itemize}

Marketing Outputs:

\item

\end{itemize}

\href{https://slideplayer.com/slide/5259893/}{\includegraphics{images/Input-Output+Model+Marketing+Actions+Inputs+Observed+Market+Outputs.jpg}}

Give phenomena for a good model:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  P1: Dynamic sales response involves a sales \textbf{growth rate} and a sales \textbf{decay rate} that are different
\item
  P2: Steady-state response can be \textbf{concave or S-shaped}. Positive sales at 0 adverting.
\item
  P3: \textbf{Competitive effects}
\item
  P4: Advertising effectiveness dynamics due to changes in media, copy, and other factors.
\item
  P5: Sales still increase or fall off even as advertising is held constant.
\end{itemize}

Saunder (1987) phenomena

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  P1: Output = 0 when Input = 0
\item
  P2: The relationship between input and output is linear
\item
  P3: Returns decrease as the scale of input increases (i.e., additional unit of input gives less output)
\item
  P4: Output cannot exceed some level (i.e., saturation)
\item
  P5: Returns increase as scale of input increases (i.e., additional unit of input gives more output)
\item
  P6: Returns first increase and then decrease as input increases (i.e., S-shaped return)
\item
  P7: Input must exceed some level before it produces any output (i.e., threshold)
\item
  P8: Beyond some level of input, output declines (i.e., supersaturation point)
\end{itemize}

\href{https://slideplayer.com/slide/4552247/}{\includegraphics{images/Response+Function+Sales+Response+Effort+Level+Max+Response+Function.jpg}}

Aggregate Response Models

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Linear model: \(Y = a + bX\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Through origin
  \item
    can only handle constant returns to scale (i.e., can't handle concave, convex, and S-shape)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  The Power Series/Polynomial model: \(Y = a + bX + c X^2 + dX^3 + ...\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    can't handle saturation and threshold
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Fraction root model/ Power model: \(Y = a+bX^c\) where c is prespecified

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    c = 1/2, called \textbf{square root model}
  \item
    c = -1, called \textbf{reciprocal model}
  \item
    c can be interpreted as elasticity if a = 0.
  \item
    c = 1, linear
  \item
    c \textless1, decreasing return
  \item
    c\textgreater1, increasing returns
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Semilog model: \(Y = a + b \ln X\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Good when constant percentage increase in marketing effort (X) result in constant absolute increase in sales (Y)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Exponential model: \(Y = ae^{bX}\) where X \textgreater0

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    b \textgreater{} 0, increasing returns and convex
  \item
    b \textless{} 0, decreasing returns and saturation
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Modified exponential model: \(Y = a(1-e^{-bX}) +c\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Decreasing returns and saturation
  \item
    upper bound = a + c
  \item
    lower bound = c
  \item
    typically used in selling effort
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Logistic model: \(Y = \frac{a}{a+ e^{-(b+cX)}}+d\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    increasing return followed by decreasing return to scale, S-shape
  \item
    saturation = a + d
  \item
    good with saturation and s-shape
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Gompertz model
\item
  ADBUDG model \citep{Little_1970} : \(Y = b + (a-b)\frac{X^c}{d + X^c}\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    c \textgreater{} 1, S-shaped
  \item
    0 \textless{} c \textless{} 1

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Concave
    \item
      saturation effect
    \item
      upper bound at a
    \item
      lower bound at b
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    typically used in advertising and selling effort.
  \item
    can handle, through origin, concave, saturation, S-shape
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Additive model for handling multiple Instruments: \(Y = af(X_1) + bg(X_2)\)
\item
  Multiplicative model for handling multiple instruments: \(Y = aX_1^b X_2^c\) where c and c are elasticities. More generally, \(Y = af(X_1)\times bg(X_2)\)
\item
  Multiplicative and additive model: \(Y = af(X_1) + bg(X_2) + cf(X_1) g(X_2)\)
\item
  Dynamic response model: \(Y_t = a_0 + a_1 X_t + \lambda Y_{t-1}\) where \(a_1\) = current effect, \(\lambda\) = carry-over effect
\end{itemize}

Dynamic Effects

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Carry-over effect: current marketing expenditure influences future sales

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Advertising adstock/ advertising carry-over is the same thing: lagged effect of advertising on sales
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Delayed-response effect: delays between when marketing investments and their impact
\item
  Customer holdout effects
\item
  Hysteresis effect
\item
  New trier and wear-out effect
\item
  Stocking effect
\end{itemize}

Simple Decay-effect model:

\[
A_t = T_t + \lambda T_{t-1}, t = 1,...,
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(A_t\) = Adstock at time t
\item
  \(T_t\) = value of advertising spending at time t
\item
  \(\lambda\) = decay/ lag weight parameter
\end{itemize}

Response Models can be characterized by:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  The number of marketing variables
\item
  whether they include competition or not
\item
  the nature of the relationship between the input variables

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\arabic{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Linear vs.~S-shape
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  whether the situation is static vs.~dynamic
\item
  whether the models reflect individual or aggregate response
\item
  the level of demand analyzed

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\arabic{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    sales vs.~market share
  \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

Market Share Model and Competitive Effects: \(Y = M \times V\) where

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Y = Brand sales models
\item
  V = product class sales models
\item
  M = market-share models
\end{itemize}

Market share (attraction) models

\[
M_i = \frac{A_i}{A_1 + ..+ A_n}
\]

where \(A_i\) attractiveness of brand i

Individual Response Model:

Multinomial logit model representing the probability of individual \texttt{i} choosing brand \texttt{l} is

\[
P_{il} = \frac{e^{A_{il}}}{\sum_j e^{A_{ij}}}
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(A_{ij}\) = attractiveness of product j for individual i \(A_{ij} = \sum_k w_k b_{ijk}\)
\item
  \(b_{ijk}\) = individual i's evaluation of product j on product attribute k, where the summation is over all the products that individual \texttt{i} is considering to purchase
\item
  \(w_k\) = importance weight associated with attribute k in forming product preferences.
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{distribution-channels}{%
\section{Distribution Channels}\label{distribution-channels}}

\citet{mcguire1983}

Assumptions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Two manufacturing (wholesaling) firms differentiated and competing products: Upstream firms (manufacturers) and downstream channel members (retailers)
\end{enumerate}

3 types of structure:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Both manufacturers with privately owned retailers (4 players: 2 manufacturers, 2 retailers)
\item
  Both vertically integrated (2 manufacturers)
\item
  Mix: one manufacturer with a private retailer, and one manufacturer with vertically integrated company store (3 players)
\end{enumerate}

Each retail outlet has a downward sloping demand curve:

\[
q_i = f_i(p_1,p_2)
\]

\textbf{Under decentralized system} (4 players), the Nash equilibrium demand curve is a function of wholesale prices:

\[
q_i^* = g_i (w_1, w_2)
\]

More rules:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Assume 2 retailers respond, but not the competing manufacturer
\end{enumerate}

And unobserved wholesale prices and market is not restrictive, and Nash equilibrium whole prices is still possible.

\textbf{Under mixed structure}, the two retailers compete, and non-integrated firm account for all responses in the market

\textbf{Under integrated structure}, this is a two-person game, where each chooses the retail price

Decision variables are prices (not quantities)

Under what conditions a manufacturer want to have intermediaries

Retail demand functions are assumed to be linear in prices

Demand functions are

\[
q_1' = \mu S [ 1 - \frac{\beta}{1 - \theta} p_1' + \frac{\beta \theta}{1- \theta}p_2']
\]

\[
q_2' = (1- \mu) S [ 1+ \frac{\beta \theta}{1- \theta} p_1' - \frac{\beta}{1- \theta} p_2']
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(0 \le \mu , \theta \le 1; \beta, S >0\)
\item
  S is a scale factor, which equals industry demand (\(q' \equiv q_1' + q_2'\)) when prices are 0.
\item
  \(\mu\) = absolute difference in demand
\item
  \(\theta\) = substutability of products (reflected by the cross elasticities), or the ratio of the rate of change of quantity with respect to the competitor's price to the rate of change of quantity with respect to own price.

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    \(\theta = 0\) means independent demands (firms are monopolists)
  \item
    \(\theta \to 1\) means maximally substitutable
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

3 more conditions:

\[
P = \{ p_1', p_2' | p_i' -m' - s' \ge 0, i = 1,2; (1-\theta) - \beta p_1' \beta \theta p_2' \ge 0, (1- \theta) + \beta \theta p_1' - \beta p_2' \ge 0 \}
\]

where \(m', s'\) are fixed manufacturing and selling costs per unit

To have a set of \(P\), then

\[
\beta \le \frac{1}{m' + s'}
\]

and to have industry demand no increase with increases in either price then

\[
\frac{\theta}{1 + \theta} \le \mu \le \frac{1}{1 + \theta}
\]

After rescaling, the industry demand is

\[
q = 2 (1- \theta) (p_1+ p_2)
\]

Results:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  When each manufacturer is a monopolist (\(\theta = 0\)), it's twice as profitable for each to sell through its own channel
\item
  When demand is maximally affected by the actions of the competing retailers (\(\theta \to 1\)), it's 3 times as profitable to have private dealers.
\item
  The breakeven point happens at \(\theta = .708\)
\item
  \textbf{In conclusion, the optimal distribution system depends of the degree of substitubability at the retail level.}
\end{itemize}

Three types of advertising:

\item
  Comparison: demand shifting away from your competitor (include complementary)
\end{enumerate}

n customers distributed uniformly along the Hotelling's line (more likely for mature market where demand doesn't change).

\[
U_A = V - p_A - tx \\
U_B = V - p_B - t(1-x)
\]

For \textbf{Persuasive} advertising (highlight the value of the product to the consumer):

\[
U_A = A_A V - p_A - tx
\]

or increase value (i.e., reservation price).

\[
U_A = \sqrt{Ad_A} V - p_A - tx
\]

or more and more customers want the product (i.e., more customers think firm A product closer to what they want)

\[
U_A = V - p_A - \frac{tx}{\sqrt{Ad_A}}
\]

\textbf{Comparison} Advertising:

\[
U_A = V - p_A - t\sqrt{Ad_{B}}x \\
U_B = V - p_B - t \sqrt{Ad_A}(1 - x)
\]

Find marginal consumers

\[
V - p_A - t\sqrt{Ad_{B}}x = V - p_B - t \sqrt{Ad_A}(1 - x)
\]

\[
x = \frac{1}{t \sqrt{Ad_A} + t \sqrt{Ad_B}} (-p_A + p_B + t \sqrt{Ad_A})
\]

then profit functions are (make sure the profit function is concave)

\[
\pi_A = p_A x n - \phi Ad_A \\
\pi_B = p_B (1-x) n - \phi Ad_B
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \(\phi\) = per unit cost of advertising (e.g., TV advertising vs.~online advertising in this case, TV advertising per unit cost is likely to be higher than online advertising per unit cost)
\item
  t can also be thought of as return on advertising (traditional Hotelling's model considers t as transportation cost)
\end{itemize}

Equilibrium prices conditioned on advertising

\[
\frac{d \pi_A}{p_A}  = - \frac{d}{p_A} () \\
\frac{d \pi_B}{p_B} = \frac{d}{p_B}
\]

Then optimal pricing solutions are

\[
p_A = \frac{2}{3} t \sqrt{Ad_A} + \frac{1}{3} t \sqrt{Ad_B} \\
p_B = \frac{1}{3} t \sqrt{Ad_A} + \frac{2}{3} t \sqrt{Ad_B}
\]

Prices increase with the intensities of advertising (if you invest more in advertising, then you charge higher prices). Each firm price is directly proportional to their advertising, and you will charger higher price when your competitor advertise as well.

Then, optimal advertising (with the optimal prices) is

\[
\frac{d \pi_A}{d Ad_A} \\
\frac{d \pi_B}{d Ad_B} 
\]

Hence, Competitive equilibrium is

\[
Ad_A = \frac{25 t^2 n^2}{576 \phi^2} \\
Ad_B = \frac{25t^2 n^2}{576 \phi^2} \\
p_A = p_B = \frac{5 t^2 n }{24 \phi}
\]

As cost of advertising (\(\phi\)), firms spend less on advertising

Higher level of return on advertising (\(t\)), firms benefit more from advertising

With advertising in the market, the equilibrium prices are higher than if there were no advertising.

Since colluding on prices are forbidden, and colluding on advertising is hard to notice, firms could potential collude on advertising (e.g., pulsing).

Assumption:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Advertising decision before pricing decision (reasonable because pricing is earlier to change, while advertising investment is determined at the beginning of each period).
\end{enumerate}

Collusive equilibrium (instead of using \(Ad_A, Ad_B\), use \(Ad\) - set both advertising investment equal):

\[
Ad_A = Ad_B = \frac{t^2 n^2}{16 \phi^2} > \frac{25t^2 n^2}{576 \phi^2}
\]

Hence, collusion can be make advertising investment equilibrium higher, which makes firms charge higher prices, and customers will be worse off. (more reference Aluf and Shy - check Modeling Seminar Folder - Advertising).

Combine both \textbf{Comparison} and \textbf{Persuasive} Advertising

\[
U_A = V - p_A - tx \frac{\sqrt{Ad_B}}{\sqrt{Ad_A}} \\
U_B = V - p_B - t(1-x) \frac{\sqrt{Ad_A}}{\sqrt{Ad_B}}
\]

\textbf{Informative} Advertising

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Increase number of n customers (more likely for new products where the number of potential customers can change)
\end{enumerate}

How do we think about customers, how much to consume. People consume more when they have more availability, and less when they have less in stock \citep{ailawadi1998}

\citet{villas-boas1993}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Under monopoly, firms would be better off to pulse (i.e., alternate advertising between a minimum level and efficient amount of advertising) because of the S-shaped of the advertising response function.
\end{itemize}

Model assumptions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The curve of the advertising response function is S-shaped
\item
  Markov strategies: what firms do in this period depends on what might affect profits today or in the future (independent of the history)
\end{enumerate}

Propositions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  ``If the loss from lowering the consideration level is larger than the efficient advertising expenditures, the unique Markov perfect equilibrium is for firms to advertise, whatever the consideration levels of both firms are.''
\end{enumerate}

\citet{nelson1974}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Quality of a brand is determined before a purchase of a brand is ``search qualities''
\item
  Quality that is not determined before a purchase is ``experience qualities''
\item
  Brand risks credibility if it advertises misleading information, and pays the costs of processing nonbuying customers
\item
  There is a reverse association between quality produced and utility adjusted price
\item
  Firms that want to sell more advertise more
\item
  Firms advertise to their appropriate audience, i.e., ``those whose tastes are best served by a given brand are those most likely to see an advertisement for that brand'' (p.~734).
\item
  Advertising for experience qualities is indirect information while advertising for search qualities is direct information . (p.~734).
\item
  Goods are classified based on quality variation (i.e., whether the quality variation was based on searhc of experience).
\item
  3 types of goods

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    experience durable
  \item
    experience nondurable
  \item
    search goods
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Experience goods are advertised more than search goods because advertisers increase sales via increasing the reputability of the sellers.
\item
  The marginal revenue of advertisement is greater for search goods than for experience goods (p.~745). Moreover, search goods will concentrate in newspapers and magazines while experience goods are seen on other media.
\item
  For experience goods, WOM is better source of info than advertising (p.~747).
\item
  Frequency of purchase moderates the differential effect of WOM and advertising (e.g., for low frequency purchases, we prefer WOM) (p.~747).
\item
  When laws are moderately enforced, deceptive advertising will happen (too little law, people would not trust, too much enforcement, advertisers aren't incentivized to deceive, but moderate amount can cause consumers to believe, and advertisers to cheat) (p.~749). And usually experience goods have more deceptive advertising (because laws are concentrated here).
\end{itemize}

\citet{iyer2005}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Firms advertise to their targeted market (those who have a strong preference for their products) than competitor loyalists, which endogenously increase differentiation in the market, and increases equilibrium profits
\item
  Targeted advertising is more valuable than target pricing. Target advertising leads to higher profits regardless whether firms have target pricing. Target pricing increased competition for comparison shoppers (no improvement in equilibrium profits). (p.~462 - 463).
\end{itemize}

Comparison shoppers size:

\[
s = 1 - 2h
\]

where \(h\) is the market size of each firm's consumers (those who prefer to buy product from that firm). Hence, \(h\) also represents the differentiation between the two firms

See table 1 (p.~469).

\(A\) is the cost for advertising the entire market

\(r\) is the reservation price

\citet{chen2009}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \emph{Combative} vs.~\emph{constructive} advertising
\item
  Informative complementary and persuasive advertising

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Informative: increase awareness, reduce search costs, increase product differentiation
  \item
    Complementary (under comparison): increase utility by signaling social prestige
  \item
    Persuasive: decrease price sensitivity (include combative)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Consumer response moderates the effect of combative adverting on price competition:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    It decreases price competition
  \item
    It increases price competition when (1) consumers preferences are biased (firms that advertise have their products favored by the consumers), (2) disfavor firms can't advertise and only respond with price. because advertising war leads to a price war (when firms want to increase their own profitability while collective outcome is worse off).
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{akerlof1970}{%
\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\citet{akerlof1970}}{@akerlof1970}}\label{akerlof1970}}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  This paper is on adverse selection
\item
  The relationship between quality and uncertainty (in automobiles market)
\item
  2 x 2 (used vs.~new, good vs.~bad)
\end{itemize}

\(q\) = probability of getting a good car = probability of good cars produced

and \((1-q)\) is the probability of getting a lemon

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Used car sellers have knowledge about the probability of the car being bad, but buyers don't. And buyers pay the same price for a lemon as for a good car (info asymmetry).
\item
  Gresham's law for good and bad money is not transferable (because the reason why bad money drives out goo d money because of even exchange rate, while buyers of a car cannot tell if it is good or bad).
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{asymmetrical-info}{%
\subsubsection{Asymmetrical Info}\label{asymmetrical-info}}

Demand for used automobiles depends on price quality:

\[
Q^d = D(p, \mu)
\]

Supply for used cars depends on price

\[
S = S(p)
\]

and average quality depends on price

\[
\mu = \mu(p)
\]

In equilibrium

\[
S(p) = D(p, \mu(p))
\]

\textbf{At no price will any trade happen}

Example:

Assume 2 groups of graders:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  First group: \(U_1 = M = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\) where

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    \(M\) is the consumption of goods other than cars
  \item
    \(x_i\) is the quality of the i-th car
  \item
    n is the number of cars
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Second group: \(U_2 = M + \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{3}{2} x_i\)
\end{enumerate}

Group 1's income is \(Y_1\)

Group 2's income is \(Y_2\)

Demand for first group is

\[
\begin{cases}
D_1 = \frac{Y_1}{p} & \frac{\mu}{p}>1 \\
D_1 = 0 & \frac{\mu}{p}<1
\end{cases}
\]

Assume we have uniform distribution of automobile quality.

Supply offered by first group is

\[
S_2 = \frac{pN}{2} ; p \le 2
\]

with average quality \(\mu = p/2\)

Demand for second group is

\[
\begin{cases}
D_2 = \frac{Y_2}{p} & \frac{3 \mu}{2} >p \\
D_2 = 0 & \frac{3 \mu}{2} < p
\end{cases}
\]

and supply by second group is \(S_2 = 0\)

Thus, total demand \(D(p, \mu)\) is

\[
\begin{cases}
D(p, \mu) = (Y_2 + Y_1) / p & \text{ if } p < \mu \\
D(p, \mu) = (Y_2)/p & \text{ if } \mu < p < 3\mu /2 \\
D(p, \mu) = 0 & \text{ if } p > 3 \mu/2
\end{cases}
\]

With price \(p\), average quality is \(p/2\), and thus at no price will any trade happen

\hypertarget{symmetric-info}{%
\subsubsection{Symmetric Info}\label{symmetric-info}}

Car quality is uniformly distributed \(0 \le x \le 2\)

Supply

\[
\begin{cases}
S(p) = N & p >1 \\
S(p) = 0
\end{cases}
\]

Demand

\[
\begin{cases}
D(p) = (Y_2 + Y_1) / p & p < 1 \\
D(p) = Y_2/p & 1 < p < 3/2 \\
D(p) = 0 & p > 3/2
\end{cases}
\]

In equilibrium

\[
\begin{cases}
p = 1 & \text{ if } Y_2< N \\
p = Y_2/N & \text{ if } 2Y_2/3 < N < Y_2 \\
p = 3/2 & \text{ if } N < 2 Y_2 <3
\end{cases}
\]

\hfill\break
This model also applies to (1) insurance case for elders (over 65), (2) the employment of minorities, (3) the costs of dishonesty, (4) credit markets in underdeveloped countries

To counteract the effects of quality uncertainty, we can have

  Guarantees

  Brand-name good

\hypertarget{spence1973}{%
\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\citet{spence1973}}{@spence1973}}\label{spence1973}}

Built on \citep{akerlof1970} model

Consider 2 employees:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Employee 1: produces 1 unit of production
\item
  Employee 2: produces 2 units of production
\end{itemize}

We have \(\alpha\) people of type 1, and \(1-\alpha\) people of type 2

Average productivity

\[
E(P) = \alpha + 2( 1- \alpha) = 2- \alpha
\]

You can signal via education.

To model cost of education,

Let E to be the cost of education for type 1

E/2 to be the cost education for type 2

If type 1 signals they are high-quality worker, then they have to go through the education and cost is E, and net utility of type 1 worker

\[
2 - E < 1 \\
E >1
\]

If type 2 signals they are high-quality worker, then they also have to go through the education and cost is E/2 and net utility of type 2 worker is

\[
2 - E/2 > 1 \\
E< 2
\]

If we keep \(1 < E < 2\), then we have separating equilibrium (to have signal credible enough of education )

\hypertarget{moorthy1995}{%
\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\citet{moorthy1995}}{@moorthy1995}}\label{moorthy1995}}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Money-back guarantee signals quality
\item
  Transaction cost are those the seller or buyer has to pay when redeeming a money-back guarantee
\item
  Money-back guarantee does not include product return (buyers have to incur expense), but guarantee a full refund of the purchase price.
\item
  If signals are costless, there is no difference between money-back guarantees and price
\item
  But signal are costly,

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Under homogeneous buyers, low-quality sellers cannot mimic high-quality sellers' strategy (i.e., money-back guarantee)
  \item
    Under heterogeneous buyers,

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      when transaction costs are too high, the seller chooses either not to use money-back guarantee strategy or signal through price.
    \item
      When transaction costs are moderate, there is a critical value of seller transaction costs where

      \begin{itemize}
      \item
        below this point, the high-quality sellers' profits increase with transaction costs
      \item
        above this point, the high-quality sellers' profits decrease with transaction costs
      \end{itemize}
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Uninformative advertising (``money-burning'') is defined as expenditures that do not affect demand directly. \textbf{is never needed}
\item
  Moral hazard:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Consumers might exhaust consumption within the money-back guarantee period
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{non-cooperative}{%
\subsection{Non-cooperative}\label{non-cooperative}}

Outline for non-cooperative bargaining

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The rules
\end{itemize}

Take-it-or-leave-it Offers

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Bargain over a cake
\item
  If you accept, we trade
\item
  If you reject, no one eats
\item
  Under perfect info, there is a simple rollback equilibrium
\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  In general, bargaining takes on a ``take-it-or-counteroffer'' procedure
\item
  If time has value, both parties prefer to trade earlier to trade later

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    E.g., labor negotiations - later agreements come at a price of strikes, work stoppages
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Delays imply less surplus left to be shared among the parties
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Two-stage bargaining}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  I offer a proportion, \(p\) , of the cake to you
\item
  If rejected, you may counteroffer (and \(\delta\) of the cake melts)
\item
  Payoffs:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    In the first period: 1-p, p
  \item
    In second period: \((1-\delta) (1-p),(1-\delta)p\)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Since period 2 is the final period, this is just like a take-it-or-leave-it offer

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    You will offer me the smallest piece that I will accept, leaving you with all of \(1-\delta\) and leaving me with almost 0
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Rollback: then in the first period: I am better off by giving player B more than what he would have in period 2 (i.e., give you at least as much surplus)
\item
  You surplus if you accept in the first period is \(p\)
\item
  Accept if: your surplus in first period greater than your surplus in second period \(p \ge 1 - \delta\)
\item
  IF there is a second stage, you get \(1 - \delta\) and I get 0
\item
  You will reject any offer in the first stage that does not offer you at least \(1 - \delta\)
\item
  In the first period, I offer you \(1 - \delta\)
\item
  Note: \textbf{the more patient you are (the slower the cake melts) the more you receive now}
\item
  Whether first or second mover has the advantage depends on \(\delta\).

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    If \(\delta\) is high (melting fast), then first mover is better.
  \item
    If \(\delta\) is low (melting slower), then second mover is better.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Either way - if both players think, agreement would be reached in the first period
\item
  In any bargaining setting, strike a deal as early as possible.
\end{itemize}

Why doesn't this happen in reality?

\begin{itemize}
\item
  reputation building
\item
  lack of information
\end{itemize}

Why bargaining doesn't happen quickly? Information asymmetry

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Likelihood of success (e.g., uncertainty in civil lawsuits)
\end{itemize}

Lessons:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Rules of the bargaining game uniquely determine the bargain outcome
\item
  which rules are better for you depends on patience, info
\item
  What is the smallest acceptable piece? Trust your intuition
\item
  delays are always less profitable: Someone must be wrong
\end{itemize}

Non-monetary Utility

\begin{itemize}
\item
  each side has a reservation price

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    LIke in civil suit: expectation of wining
  \end{itemize}
\item
  The reservation price is unknown
\item
  One must:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    probabilistically determine best offer
  \item
    but - probability implies a chance that non bargain will take place
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Example:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Company negotiates with a union
\item
  Two types of bargaining:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Union makes a take-it-or-leave-it offer
  \item
    Union makes a n offer today. If it's rejected, the Union strikes, then makes another offer

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      A strike costs the company 10\% of annual profits.
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Probability that the company is ``highly profitable'', ie., 200k is \(p\)
\item
  If offer wage of \$150k

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Definitely accepted
  \item
    Expected wage = \$150K
  \end{itemize}
\item
  If offer wage of \$200K

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Accepted with probability \(p\)
  \item
    Expected wage = \$200k(p)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \(p = .9\) (90\% chance company is highly profitable

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    best offer: ask for \$200K wage
  \item
    Expected value of offer: \(.9 *200= 180\)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \(p = .1\) (10\% chance company is highly profitable

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    best offer: ask for \$200K wage
  \item
    Expected value of offer: \(.1 *200= 20\)
  \item
    If ask for \$10k, get \$150k
  \item
    not worth the risk to ask for more
  \end{itemize}
\item
  If first-period offer is rejected: A strike costs the company 10\% of annual profits
\item
  Strike costs a high-value company more than a low value company
\item
  Use this fact to screen
\item
  What if the union asks for \$170k in the first period?

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Low profit firms (\$150k) rejects - as can't afford to take
  \item
    HIgh profit firm must guess what will happen if it rejects

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      Best case: union strikes and then asks for only \$140k (willing to pay for some cost of strike), but not all)
    \item
      In the mean time: strike cost the company \$20K
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  High-profit firm accepts
\end{itemize}

Separating equilibrium

\begin{itemize}
\item
  only high-profit firms accept the first period
\item
  If offer is rejected, Union knows that it is facing a low-profit firm
\item
  Ask for \$140k
\end{itemize}

What's happening

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Union lowers price after a rejection

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Looks like giving in
  \item
    looks like bargaining
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Actually, the union is screening its bargaining partner

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Different ``types'' of firms have different values for the future
  \item
    Use these different values to screen
  \item
    Time is used as a screening device
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{nash1950}{%
\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\citet{nash1950}}{@nash1950}}\label{nash1950}}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Bargaining, bilateral monopoly (nonzero-sum two -person game).
\item
  Non action taken by one individual (without the consent of the other) can affect the other's gain.
\item
  Assumptions:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Rational individuals (maximize gain)
  \item
    Full knowledge: tastes and preferences are known
  \item
    Transitive Ordering: \(A>C\) when \(A>B\), \(B>C\). Also related to substitutability if two events are of equal probability
  \item
    Continuity assumption
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Properties:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    \(u(A) > u(B)\) means A is more desirable than B where \(u\) is a utility function
  \item
    Linearity property: If \(0 \le p \le 1\), then \(u(pA + (1-p)B) = pu(A) + (1-p)u(B)\)

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      For two person: \(p[A,B] + (1-p)[C,D] = [pA - (1-p)C, pB + (1-p)D]\)
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Anticipation = \(p A - (1-p) B\) where

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    \(p\) is the prob of getting A
  \item
    A and B are two events.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\(u_1, u_2\) are utility function

\(c(s)\) is the solution point in a set S (compact, convex, with 0)

Assumptions:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  If \(\alpha \in S\) s.t there is \(\beta \in S\) where \(u_1(\beta) > u_2(\alpha)\) and \(u_2(\beta) > u_2(\alpha)\) then \(\alpha \neq c(S)\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    People try to maximize utility
  \end{itemize}
\item
  If \(S \in T\) , c(T) is in S then \(c(T) = c(S)\)
\item
  If S is symmetric with respect to the line \(u_1 = u_2\), then \(c(S)\) is on the line \(u_1 = u_2\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Equality of bargaining
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
