\hypertarget{pricing-and-search-theory}{%
\section{Pricing and Search Theory}\label{pricing-and-search-theory}}

\hypertarget{varian1980}{%
\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\citet{varian1980}}{@varian1980}}\label{varian1980}}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  From Stigler's seminar paper \citep{stiglitz1982, salop1977}, model of equilibrium price dispersion is born

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Spatial price dispersion: assume uninformed and informed consumers

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      Since consumers can learn from experience, the result does not hold over time
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    Temporal price dispersion: sales
  \end{itemize}
\item
  This paper is based on

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Stiglitz: assume informed (choose lowest price store) and uninformed consumers (choose stores at random)
  \item
    Shilony \citep{shilony1977}: randomized pricing strategies
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\(I >0\) is the number of informed consumers

\(M >0\) is the number of uninformed consumers

\(n\) is the number of stores

\(U = M/n\) is the number of uninformed consumers per store

Each store has a density function \(f(p)\) indicating the prob it charges price \(p\)

Stores choose a price based on \(f(p)\)

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Succeeds if it has the lowest price among n prices, then it has \(I + U\) customers
\item
  Fails then only has \(U\) customers
\item
  Stores charge the same lowest price will share equal size of informed customers
\end{itemize}

\(c(q)\) is the cost curve

\(p^* = \frac{c(I+U)}{(I+U}\) is the average cost with the maximum number of customers a store can get

Prop 1: \(f(p) = 0\) for \(p >r\) or \(p < p^*\)

Prop 2: No symmetric equilibrium when stores charge the same price

Prop 3: No point masses in the equilibrium pricing strategies

Prop 4: If \(f(p) >0\), then

\[
\pi_s(p) (1-F(p))^{n-1} + \pi_f (p) [1-(1-F(p))^{n-1}] =0
\]

Prop 5: \(\pi_f (p) (\pi_f(p) - \pi_s (p))\) is strictly decreasing in \(p\)

Prop 6: \(F(p^* _ \epsilon) >0\) for any \(\epsilon> 0\)

Prop 7: \(F(r- \epsilon) <1\) for any \(\epsilon > 0\)

Prop 8: No gap \((p_1, p_2)\) where \(f(p) \equiv 0\)

Decision to be informed can be endogenous, and depends on the ``full price'' (search costs + fixed cost)

\hypertarget{lazear1984}{%
\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\citet{lazear1984}}{@lazear1984}}\label{lazear1984}}

Retail pricing and clearance sales

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Goods' characteristics affect pricing behaviors
\item
  Market's thinness can affect price volatility
\item
  Relationship between uniqueness of a goods and its price
\item
  Price reduction policies as a function of shelf time
\end{itemize}

Set up

Single period model

\(V\) = the price of the only buyer who is willing to purchase the product

\(f(V)\) is the density of V (firm's prior)

\(F(V)^2\) is its distribution function

Firms try to

\[
\underset{R}{\operatorname{max}} R[1 - F(R)]
\]

where \(R\) is the price

\(1 - F(R)\) is the prob that \(V > R\)

Assume \(V\) is uniform \([0,1]\) then

\(F(R) = R\) so that the optimum is \(R = 0.5\) with expected profits of \(0.25\)

Two-period model

Failures in period 1 implies \(V<R_1\).

Hence, based on Bayes' theorem, the posterior distribution in period 2 is \([0, R_1]\)

\(F_2(V) = V/R_1\) (posterior distribution)

\(R_1\) affect (1) sales in period 1, (2) info in period 2

Then, firms want to choose \(R_1, R_2\) .Firms try to

\[
\underset{R_1, R_2}{\operatorname{max}} R_1[1 - F(R_1)] + R_2 [1-F_2(R_2)]F(R_1)
\]

Then, in period 2, the firms try to

\[
\underset{R_2}{\operatorname{max}} R_2[1 - F_2(R_2)]
\]

Based on Bayes' Theorem

\[
F_2(R_2) =
\begin{cases}
F(R_2)/ F(R_1) & \text{for } R_2 < R_1 \\
1 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

Due to FOC, second period price is always lower than first price price

Expected profits are higher than that of one-period due to higher expected probability of a sale in the two-period problem.

But this model assume

\begin{itemize}
\item
  no brand recognition
\item
  no contagion or network effects
\end{itemize}

In thin markets and heterogeneous consumers

we have \(N\) customers examine the good with the prior probability \(P\) of being shoppers, and \(1-P\) being buyers who are willing to buy at \(V\)

There are 3 types of people

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  customers = all those who inspect the good
\item
  buyers = those whose value equal \(V\)
\item
  shoppers = those who value equal \(0\)
\end{enumerate}

An individual does not know if he or she is a buyer or shopper until he or she is a customer (i.e., inspect the goods)

Then, firms try to

\[
\begin{aligned}
\underset{R_1, R_2}{\operatorname{max}} &  R_1(\text{prob sale in 1}) + R_2 (\text{Posterior prob sale in 2})\times (\text{Prob no sale in 1}) \\
& R_1 \times (- F(R_1))(1-P^N) + R_2 \{ (1-F_2(R_2))(1- P^N) \} \times \{ 1 - [(1 - F(R_1))(1-P^N)] \}
\end{aligned}
\]

Based on Bayes' Theorem, the density for period 2 is

\[
f_2(V) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{R_1 (1- P^N) + P^N} \text{ for } V \le R_1 \\
\frac{P^N}{R_1 (1- P^N) + P^N} \text{ for } V > R_1
\end{cases}
\]

Conclusion:

As \(P^N \to 1\) (almost all customers are shoppers), there is not much info to be gained. Hence, 2-period is no different than 2 independent one-period problems. Hence, the solution in this case is identical to that of one-period problem.

When \(P^N\) is small, prices start higher and fall more rapid as time unsold increases

When \(P^N \to 1\), prices tend to be constant.

\(P^N\) can also be thought of as search cost and info.

Observable Time patterns of price and quantity

Pricing is a function of

\begin{itemize}
\item
  The number of customers \(N\)
\item
  The proportion of shoppers \(P\)
\item
  The firm's beliefs about the market (parameterized through the prior on \(V\))
\end{itemize}

Markets where prices fall rapidly as time passes, the probability that the good will go unsold is low.

Goods with high initial price are likely to sell because high initial price reflects low \(P^N\) - low shoppers

Heterogeneity among goods

The more disperse prior leads to a higher expected price for a given mean. And because of longer time on shelf, expected revenues for such a product can be lower.

Fashion, Obsolescence, and discounting the future

The more obsolete, the more anxious is the seller

Goods that are ``classic'', have a higher initial price, and its price is less sensitive to inventory (compared to fashion goods)

Discounting is irrelevant to the pricing condition due to constant discount rate (not like increasing obsolescence rate)

For non-unique good, the solution is identical to that of the one-period problem.

Simple model

Customer's Valuation \(\in [0,1]\)

Firm's decision is to choose a price \(p\) (label - \(R_1\))

One-period model

Buy if \(V >R_1\) prob = \(1-R_1\)

Not buy if \(V<R_1\) probability = \(R_1\)

\(\underset{R_1}{\operatorname{max}} [R_1][1-R_1]\) hence, FOC \(R_1 = 1/2\), then total \(\pi = 1/2-(1/2)^2 = 1/4\)

Two-period model

Two prices \(R_1, R_2\)

\(R_1 \in [0,1]\)

\(R_2 \in [0, R_1]\)

\[
\underset{R_1}{\operatorname{max}} [R_1][1-R_1] + R_2 (1 - R_2)(R_1)
\]

\[
\underset{R_1}{\operatorname{max}} [R_2][\frac{R_1 - R_2}{R_1}]
\]

FOC \(R_2 = R_1/2\)

\[
\underset{R_1}{\operatorname{max}} R_1(1-R_1)  + \frac{R_1}{2}(1 - \frac{R_1}{2}) (R_1)
\]

FOC: \(R_1 = 2/3\) then \(R_2 = 1/3\)

\(N\) customers

Each customer could be a

\begin{itemize}
\item
  shopper with probability p with \(V <0\)
\item
  buyer with probability \(1-p\) with \(V > \text{price}\)
\end{itemize}

Modify equation 1 to incorporate types of consumers

\[
R_1(1 - R_1)(1- p^N) + R_2 (1- R_2) R_1 (1-p^N) [ 1 - (1-R_1)(1-p^N)]
\]

Reduce costs by

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Economy of scale \(c(\text{number of units})\)
\item
  Economy of scope \(c(\text{number of types of products})\) (typically, due to the transfer of knowledge)
\item
  Experience effect \(c(\text{time})\) (is a superset of economy of scale)
\end{itemize}

\citet{lal1999}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Conventional idea: lower search cost (e.g., Internet) will increase price competition.
\item
  Assumptions:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Demand side: info about product attributes:

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      digital attributes (those can be communicated via the Internet)
    \item
      nondigital attributes (those can't)
    \end{itemize}
  \item

  \end{itemize}
\item

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    high proportion of Internet users
  \item
    Not overwhelming nondigital attributes
  \item
    Favor familiar brands
  \item
    destination shopping
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Monopoly pricing can lead to higher prices and discourage consumer from searching
\item
  Stores serve as acquiring tools, while Internet maintain loyal customers.
\end{itemize}

\citet{kuksov2004}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  For products that cannot be changed easily (design),lower search costs lead to \textbf{higher price competition}
\item
  For those that can be easily changed, lower search costs lead to higher product differentiation, which in turn \textbf{decreases price competition}, lower social welfare, higher industry profits.
\end{itemize}

\citep{salop1977}

30 years back, few companies use price promotions

Effects of Short-term price discounts

\begin{itemize}
\item
  measured effects (84\%) \citep{gupta1988}

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Brand switching (14\%)
  \item
    purchase acceleration (2\%)
  \item
    quantity purchased
  \item
    elasticity of ST price changes is an order of magnitude higher
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Other effects:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    general trial (traditional reason)
  \item
    encourages consumers to carry inventory hence increase consumption
  \item
    higher sales of complementary products
  \item
    small effect on store switching
  \item
    Asymmetric effect (based on brand strength) (bigger firms always benefit more)

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      expect of store brands
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Negative Effects

\begin{itemize}

  Expectations of future promotions
\item
  Lowering of Reference Price
\item
  Increase in price sensitivity

\end{itemize}

Trade Discounts

Short-term discounts offered to the trade:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Advantages

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Incentivize the trade to push our product
  \item
    gets attention of sales force
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Disadvantages

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    might not be passed onto the consumer
  \item
    trade forward buys (hurts production plans)
  \item
    hard to forecast demand
  \item
    trade expects discounts in the future (cost of doing business)
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Scanback can help increase retail pass through (i.e., encourage retailers to have consumer discounts)

Determinants of pass through

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Higher when

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Consumer elasticity is higher
  \item
    promoting brand is stronger
  \item
    shape of the demand function
  \item
    lower frequency of promotions
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

(Online) Shelf-price discounts \citep{raju1990}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If you are a stronger brand you can discount infrequently because the weaker brands cannot predict when the stronger brands will promote. Hence, it has to promote more frequently
\end{itemize}

\item
  The ability of cents-off coupons to price distribution has reduced considerably because of their very wide availability

Coupon Design

\begin{itemize}

  Expiration dates

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Long vs short expiration dates: Stronger brands should have shorter windows (because a lot more of your loyalty customer base will utilize the coupons).
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Method of distribution

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    In-store (is better)
  \item
    Through the package
  \item

  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Package Coupons acquisition and retention trade-offs

3 types of package coupons:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Peel-off (lots more use the coupons) lowest profits for the firm
\item
  in-packs (fewer customers will buy the products in the first period)
\item
  on-packs (customers buy the products and they redeem in the next period) \textbf{best approach}
\end{itemize}

Summary

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Trade and consumer promotion are necessary
\item
  Consumer promotion (avoid shelf price discount/news paper coupons, use package coupons
\item
  strong interaction between advertising and promotion (area for more research)
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{narasimhan1988b}{%
\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\citet{narasimhan1988b}}{@narasimhan1988b}}\label{narasimhan1988b}}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Marketing tools to promote products:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Advertising
  \item
    Trade promotions
  \item
    Consumer promotions
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Pricing promotions:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Price deals
  \item
    Cents-off labels
  \item
    coupons
  \item
    Rebates
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Brand loyalty can help explain the variation in prices (in competitive markets)
\item
  Firms try to make optimal trade-off between

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    attracting brand switchers
  \item
    loss of profits from loyal customers.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Deviation from the maximum price = promotion
\end{itemize}

Assumptions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Firms with identical products, and cost structures (constant or declining). Non-cooperative game.
\item
  Same reservation price
\item
  Three consumer segments:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\arabic{enumii}.}
  \item
    Loyal to firm 1 with size \(\alpha_1 (0<\alpha_1<1)\)
  \item
    Loyal to firm 2 with size \(\alpha_2(0 < \alpha_2 < \alpha_1)\) \textbf{(asymmetric firm)}
  \item
    Switchers with size \(\beta (0 < \beta = 1 - \alpha_1 - \alpha_2)\)
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  Costless price change, no intertemporal effects (in quantity or loyalty)
\end{enumerate}

To model \(\beta\) either

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(d \in (-b, a)\) is switch cost (individual parameter)
\end{enumerate}

\[
\begin{cases}
\text{buy brand 1} & \text{if } P_1 \le P_2 - d \\
\text{buy brand 2} & \text{if } P_1 > P_2 - d 
\end{cases}
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Identical switchers (same d)
\item
  \(d = 0\) (extremely price sensitive)
\end{enumerate}

For case 1, there is a pure strategy, while case 2 and 3 have no pure strategies, only mixed strategies

Details for case 3:

Profit function

\[
\Pi_i (P_i, P_j) = \alpha_i P_i + \delta_{ij} \beta P_i
\]

where

\[
\delta_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{ if } P_i < P_j \\
1/2 & \text{ if } P_i = P_j \\
0 & \text{ if } P_i > P_j
\end{cases}
\]

and \(i = 1,2, i \neq j\)

Prop 1: no pure Nash equilibrium

Mixed Strategy profit function

\[
\Pi_i (P_i) = \alpha_i P_i + Prob(P_j > P_i) \beta P_i + Prob (P_j = P_i) \frac{\beta}{2} P_i
\]

where \(P_i \in S_i^*, i \neq j; i , j = 1, 2\)

Then the expected profit functions of the two-player game is

\[
\underset{F_i}{\operatorname{max}} E(\Pi_i) = \int \Pi_i (P_i) d F_i (P_i)
\]

\(P_i \in S_i^*\)

such that

\[
\Pi_i \ge \alpha_i r \\
\int dF_i (P_i) = 1 \\
P_i \in S_i^*
\]

\begin{itemize}

To assess nonoptimality, following \citet{basu1990}

Moral hazard: cannot assess salesperson's true effort.

Assumptions:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  The salesperson reacts to the compensation scheme by deciding on an effort level that maximizes his overall utility, i.e., the expected utility from the (stochastic) compensation minus the effort distuility.
\item
  Firm wants to maximize its profit
\item
  compensation is greater than saleperson's alternative.
\item
  Dollar sales \(x_i \sim Gamma\) (because sales are non-negative and standard deviation getting proportionately larger as the mean increases) with density \(f_i(x_i|t_i)\)
\end{itemize}

Expected sales per period

\[
E[x_i |t_i] = h_i + k_i t_i , (h_i > 0, k_i >0)
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(h_i\) = base sales level
\item
  \(k_i\) = effectiveness of effort
\end{itemize}

and \(1/\sqrt{c}\) = uncertainty in sales (coefficient of variation) = standard deviation / mean where \(c \to \infty\) means perfect certainty

salesperson's overall utility

\[
U_i[s_i(x_i)] - V_i(t_i) = \frac{1}{\delta_i}[s_i (x_i)]^{\delta_i} - d_i t_i^{\gamma_i}
\] where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(0 < \delta_i <1\) (greater \(\delta\) means less risk-averse salesperson)
\item
  \(\gamma_i >1\) (greater \(\gamma\) means more effort)
\item
  \(V_i(t_i) = d_i t_i^{\gamma_i}\) is the increasing disutility function (convex)
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{mixed-strategies}{%
\section{Mixed Strategies}\label{mixed-strategies}}

Games with finite number, and finite strategy for each player, there will always be a Nash equilibrium (might not be pure Nash, but always mixed)

Extended game

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Suppose we allow each player to choose randomizing strategies
\item
  For example, the server might serve left half of the time, and right half of the time
\item
  In general, suppose the server serves left a fraction \(p\) of the time
\item
  What is the receiver's best response?
\end{itemize}

Best Responses

If \(p = 1\), the receiver should defend to the left

\(p = 0\), the receiver should defend to the right

The expected payoff to the receiver is

\(p \times 3/4 + (1-p) \times 1/4\) if defending left

\(p \times 1/4 + (1-p) \times 3/4\) if defending right

Hence, she should defend left if

\(p \times 3/4 - (1-p)\times 1/4 > p \times 1/4 + (1-p) \times 3/4\)

We said to defend left whenever

\[
p \times 3/4 - (1-p)\times 1/4 > p \times 1/4 + (1-p) \times 3/4
\]

Server's Best response

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Suppose that the receiver goes left with probability \(q\)
\item
  if \(q = 1\), the server should serve right
\item
  If \(q = 0\), the server should server left
\item
  Hence, serve left if \(1/4 \times q + 3/4 \times (1-q) > 3/4\times q + 1/4 \times (1-q)\)
\item
  Simplifying, he should serve left if \(q < 1/2\)
\end{itemize}

Mixed strategy equilibrium:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  A mixed strategy equilibrium is a pair of mixed strategies that are mutual best responses
\item
  In the tennis example, this occurred when each play chose a 50-50 mixture of left and right
\item
  Your best strategy is when you make the option given to your opponent is obsolete.
\item
  A player chooses his strategy to make his rival indifferent
\item
  A player earns the same expected payoff for each pure strategy chosen with positive probability
\item
  Important property: When player's own payoff form a pure strategy goes up (or down), his mixture does not change.
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{market-entry-and-diffusion}{%
\section{Market Entry and Diffusion}\label{market-entry-and-diffusion}}

Product Life Cycle model

\citet{Bass_1969}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Discussion of sales has 2 types

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Innovators
  \item
    Imitators
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\(p\) = coefficient of innovation (fraction of innovators of the untapped market who buy in that period)

\(q\) = coefficient of imitation (fraction of the interaction which lead to sales in that period)

\(M\) = market potential

\(N(t)\) = cumulative sales till time \(t\)

\(M - N(t)\) = the untapped market

Sales in any time is People buying because of the pure benefits of the product, plus people buy the product after interacting with people who owned the product.

\[
S(t) = p(M- N(t)) + q \frac{N(t)}{M} [M-N(t)] \\
= pM + (q-p) N(t) - \frac{q}{M} [N(t)]^2
\]

one can estimate \(p,q,M\) from data

\(q > p\) (coefficient of imitation \textgreater{} coefficient of innovation) means that you have life cycle (bell-shaped curve)

\citet{golder1993}

Previous use

\begin{itemize}
\item
  limited databases (PIM and ASSESOR) \citep{urban1986}
\item
  exclusion of nonsurvivors
\item
  single-informant self-report
\end{itemize}

New dataset overcomes these limitations and show 50\% of the market pioneers fail, and their mean share is much lower

Early market leaders have greater long-term success and enter on average 13 years after pioneers.

Definitions (p.~159)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Inventor: firms that develop patent or important technologies in a new product category
\item
  Product pioneer: the first firm to develop a working model or sample in a new product category
\item
  Market pioneer is the first firm to sell in a new product category
\item
  Product category: a group of close substitutes
\end{enumerate}

\citet{boulding2003}

At the business level, being the leader can give you long-term profit disadvantage from the samples of consumer and industrial goods.

First-to-market leads to an initial profit advantage, which last about 12 to 14 years before becoming long-term disadvantage.

Consumer learning (education), market position (strong vs.~weak) and patent protection can moderate the effect of first-mover on profit.

\citet{golder2004}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Research on product life cycle (PLC)
\item
  Consumer durables typically grow 45 per year over 8 years, then slowdown when sales decline by 15\%, and stay below those of the previous peak for 5 years.
\item
  Slowdown typically happens when the product penetrates 35-50\% of the market
\item
  large sales increases (at first) will have larger sales declines (at slowdown).
\item
  Leisure-enhancing products tend to have higher growth rate and shorter growth stages than non leisure-enhancing products
\item
  Time-saving products have lower growth rates and longer growth stages than non time-saving products
\item
  Lower likelihood of slowdown correlates with steeper price reduction, lower penetration, and higher economic growth
\item
  A hazard model gives reasonable prediction of the slowdown and takeoff.
\end{itemize}

\citet{vandenbulte2007}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Innovations market have two segments:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Influentials: aware of new developments an affect imitators
  \item
    Imitators: model after influentials.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  This market structure is reasonable because it exhibits consistent evidence with the prior research and market (e.g., dip between the early and later parts fo the diffusion curve).
\item
  '' Erroneously specifying a mixed-influence model to a mixture process where influentials act independently from each other can generate systematic changes in the parameter values reported in earlier research.''
\item
  Two-segments model performs better than the standard mixed-influence, the Gamma/Shifted Gompertz, the Weibull-Gamma models, and similar to the Karmeshu-Goswami mixed influence model.
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{principal-agent-models-and-salesforce-compensation-1}{%
\section{Principal-Agent Models and Salesforce Compensation}\label{principal-agent-models-and-salesforce-compensation-1}}

Key Question:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Ensuring agents exert effort
\item
  Design compensation plans such that workers exert high effort?
\end{enumerate}

Designing contracts:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Effort can be monitored
\item
  Monitoring costs are too high
\end{itemize}

Timing

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Manger designs the construct
\item
  manager offers the construct and worker chooses to accept
\item
  Worker decides the extent of effort
\item
  Outcome is observed and wage is given to the worker
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Scenario 1}: Certainty

e = effort put in by worker

2 levels of e

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  2 if he works hard
\item
  0 if he shirks
\end{itemize}

Reservation utility = 10 (other alternative: can work somewhere else, or private money allows them not to work)

Agent's Utility

\[
U = 
\begin{cases}
w - e & \text{if he exerts effort e} \\
10 & \text{if he works somewhere else}
\end{cases}
\]

Revenue is a function of effort

\[
R(e) = 
\begin{cases}
H & \text{if } e = 2 \\
L & \text{if } e = 0
\end{cases}
\]

Contract

\(w^H\) = wage if \(R(e) = H\)

\(w^L\) = wage if \(R(e) = L\)

Constraints:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Worker has to participate in this labor market - participation constraint \(w^H - 2 \ge 10\)
\item
  Incentive compatibility constraint (ensure that the works always put in the effort and the manager always pay for the higher wage): \(w^H - 2 \ge w^L -0\)
\end{itemize}

Hence,

\[
w^H = 12 \\
w^L = 10
\]

Thus, contract is simple because of monitoring

\textbf{Scenario 2}: Under uncertainty

\[
R(2) = 
\begin{cases}
H & \text{w/ prob 0.8} \\
L & \text{w/ prob 0.2}
\end{cases}
\\
R(0) = 
\begin{cases}
H & \text{w/ prob 0.4} \\
L & \text{w/ prob 0.6}
\end{cases}
\]

Agent Utility

\[
U = 
\begin{cases}
E(w) - e & \text{if effort e is put} \\
10 & \text{if they choose outside option}
\end{cases}
\]

Constraints:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Participation Constraint: \(0.8w^H + 0.2w^L -2 \ge 10\)
\item
  Incentive compatibility constraint: \(0.8w^H + 0.2w^L - 2 \ge 0.4 w^H + 0.6w^L - 0\)
\end{itemize}

Thus,

\[
w^H = 13 \\
w^L = 8
\]

Expected wage bill that the manager has to pay:

\[
13\times 0.8 + 8 \times 0.2 = 12
\]

Hence, the expected money the manager has to pay is the same for both cases (certainty vs.~uncertainty)

\textbf{Scenario 3}: Asymmetric Information

Degrees of risk aversion

Manger perspective

\[
R(2) = 
\begin{cases}
H & \text{w/ prob 0.8} \\
L & \text{w/ prob 0.2}
\end{cases}
\]

Worker perspective (the number for worker is always lower, because they are more risk averse, managers are more risk neural) (the manager also knows this).

\[
R(2) = 
\begin{cases}
H & \text{w/ prob 0.7} \\
L & \text{w/ prob 0.3}
\end{cases}
\]

Participation Constraint

\[
0.7w^H + 0.3w^L - 2 \ge 10
\]

Incentive Compatibility Constraint

\[
0.6 w^H + 0.3 w^L - 2 \ge 0.4 w^H + 0.6 w^L - 0 
\]

(take R(0) from scenario 2)

\[
0.7 w^H + 0.3 w^L = 12 \\
0.3w^H - 0.3w^L = 2
\]

Hence,

\[
w^H = 14 \\
w^L = 22/3
\]

Expected wage bill for the manager is

\[
14 * 0.8 + 22/3*0.2 = 12.66
\]

Hence, expected wage bill is higher than scenario 2

Risk aversion from the worker forces the manager to pay higher wage

Dimensions that affect the proportion of salary tot total pay (p.~270, table 1)

Previous research assumes deterministic relationship between sales and effort, but this study says otherwise (stochastic relationship between sales and effort).

Assumptions:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Firm: Risk neutral: maximize expected profits
\item
  Salesperson: Risk averse . Hence, diminishing marginal utility for income \(U(s) \ge 0; U'(s) >0, U''(s) <0\)
\item
  Expected utility of the salesperson for this job \textgreater{} alternative
\item
  Utility function of the salesperson: additively separable: \(U(s) - V(t)\) where \(s\) = salary, and \(t\) = effort (time)
\item
  Marginal disutility for effort increases with effort \(V(t) \ge 0, V'(t)>0, V''(t) >0\)
\item
  Constant marginal cost of production and distribution \(c\)
\item
  Known utility function and sales-effort response function (both principal and agent)
\item
  dollar sales \(x \sim Gamma, Binom\)
\end{itemize}

Expected profit for the firm

\[
\pi = \int[(1-c)x - s(x)]f(x|t)dx
\]

Objective of the firm is to

\[
\underset{s(x)}{\operatorname{max}} \int[(1-c)x - s(x)]f(x|t)dx
\]

subject to (agent's best alternative e.g., other job offer - \(m\))

\[
\int [U(s(x))]f(x|t) dx - V(t) \ge m
\]

and the agent wants to maximize the the utility

\[
\underset{t}{\operatorname{max}} \int [U(s(x))]f(x|t)dx - V(t)
\]

\hypertarget{ordered-shapley}{%
\subsection{Ordered Shapley}\label{ordered-shapley}}

Based on \citep{Zhao_2018} (to access \href{https://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/1804/1804.05327.pdf}{paper} ) Cooperative game theory: look at the marginal contribution of each player in the game, where \textbf{Shapley value} (i..e, the credit assigned to each individual) is the expected value value of the marginal contribution over all possible permutations (e.g., all possible sequences) of the players.

Shapely value considered:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  marginal contribution of each player (i.e., channel)
\item
  sequence of joining the coalition (i.e., customer journey).
\end{itemize}

Typically, we can't apply the Shapley Value method due to computational burden (you need all possible permutations). And a drawback is that all the credit must be divided among your channels, if you have missing channels, then it will distort the estimates of other channels' estimates.

It's hard to use Shapley value model for model comparison since we have no ``ground truth''

Marketing application:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \href{https://salesforceben.com/the-drip/complete-overview-of-pardot-einstein-features/}{Pardot Einstein features} and \href{https://www.salesforceben.com/the-drip/pardot-einstein-attribution-a-deeper-dive/}{more}
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{markov-model}{%
\subsection{Markov Model}\label{markov-model}}

Markov chains maps the movement and gives a probability distribution, for moving from one state to another state. A Markov Chain has three properties:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{State space} -- set of all the states in which process could potentially exist
\item
  \textbf{Transition operator} --the probability of moving from one state to other state
\item
  \textbf{Current state probability distribution} -- probability distribution of being in any one of the states at the start of the process
\end{itemize}

In mathematically sense

\[
w_{ij}= P(X_t = s_j|X_{t-1}=s_i),0 \le w_{ij} \le 1, \sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij} =1 \forall i
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The Transition Probability (\(w_{ij}\)) = The Probability of the Previous State ( \(X_{t-1}\)) Given the Current State (\(X_t\))
\item
  The Transition Probability (\(w_{ij}\)) is No Less Than 0 and No Greater Than 1
\item
  The Sum of the Transition Probabilities Equals 1 (i.e., Everyone Must Go Somewhere)
\end{itemize}

To examine a particular node in the Markov graph, we use \textbf{removal effect} (\(s_i\)) to see its contribution to a conversion. In another word, the Removal Effect is the probability of converting when a step is completely removed; all sequences that had to go through that step are now sent directly to the null node

Each node is called \textbf{transition states}\\
The probability of moving from one channel to another channel is called \textbf{transition probability}.

first-order or ``memory-free'' Markov graph is called ``memory-free'' because the probability of reaching one state depends only on the previous state visited.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Order 0: Do not care about where the you came from or what step the you are on, only the probability of going to any state.
\item
  Order 1: Looks back zero steps. You are currently at a state. The probability of going anywhere is based on being at that step.
\item
  Order 2: Looks back one step. You came from state A and are currently at state B. The probability of going anywhere is based on where you were and where you are.
\item
  Order 3: Looks back two steps. You came from state A after state B and are currently at state C. The probability of going anywhere is based on where you were and where you are.
\item
  Order 4: Looks back three steps. You came from state A after B after C and are currently at state D. The probability of going anywhere is based on where you were and where you are.
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{example-2}{%
\subsubsection{Example 2}\label{example-2}}

Example code by \href{https://www.analyzecore.com/2016/08/03/attribution-model-r-part-1/}{Sergey Bryl'}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(dplyr)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(reshape2)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(ggplot2)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(ggthemes)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(ggrepel)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(RColorBrewer)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(ChannelAttribution)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(markovchain)}
 
\DocumentationTok{\#\#\#\#\# simple example \#\#\#\#\#}
\CommentTok{\# creating a data sample}
\NormalTok{df1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{path =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}c1 \textgreater{} c2 \textgreater{} c3\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}c1\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}c2 \textgreater{} c3\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{conv =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{conv\_null =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}
 
\CommentTok{\# calculating the model}
\NormalTok{mod1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{markov\_model}\NormalTok{(df1,}
                    \AttributeTok{var\_path =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}path\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}
                    \AttributeTok{var\_conv =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}conv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}
                    \AttributeTok{var\_null =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}conv\_null\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}
                    \AttributeTok{out\_more =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{)}
 
\CommentTok{\# extracting the results of attribution}
\NormalTok{df\_res1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ mod1}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{result}
 
\CommentTok{\# extracting a transition matrix}
\NormalTok{df\_trans1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ mod1}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{transition\_matrix}
\NormalTok{df\_trans1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{dcast}\NormalTok{(df\_trans1, channel\_from }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ channel\_to, }\AttributeTok{value.var =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}transition\_probability\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
 
\DocumentationTok{\#\#\# plotting the Markov graph }\AlertTok{\#\#\#}
\NormalTok{df\_trans }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ mod1}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{transition\_matrix}
 
\CommentTok{\# adding dummies in order to plot the graph}
\NormalTok{df\_dummy }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{channel\_from =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(start)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(conversion)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(null)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{),}
                       \AttributeTok{channel\_to =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(start)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(conversion)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(null)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{),}
                       \AttributeTok{transition\_probability =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{df\_trans }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{rbind}\NormalTok{(df\_trans, df\_dummy)}
 
\CommentTok{\# ordering channels}
\NormalTok{df\_trans}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{channel\_from }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(df\_trans}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{channel\_from,}\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(start)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(conversion)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(null)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}c1\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}c2\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}c3\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{df\_trans}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{channel\_to }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(df\_trans}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{channel\_to,}\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(start)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(conversion)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(null)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}c1\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}c2\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}c3\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{df\_trans }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{dcast}\NormalTok{(df\_trans, channel\_from }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ channel\_to, }\AttributeTok{value.var =}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}transition\_probability\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
 
\CommentTok{\# creating the markovchain object}
\NormalTok{trans\_matrix }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{matrix}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{data =} \FunctionTok{as.matrix}\NormalTok{(df\_trans[, }\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]),}\AttributeTok{nrow =} \FunctionTok{nrow}\NormalTok{(df\_trans[, }\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]), }\AttributeTok{ncol =} \FunctionTok{ncol}\NormalTok{(df\_trans[, }\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]),}\AttributeTok{dimnames =} \FunctionTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{as.character}\NormalTok{(df\_trans[,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])),}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{colnames}\NormalTok{(df\_trans[, }\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]))))}
\NormalTok{trans\_matrix[}\FunctionTok{is.na}\NormalTok{(trans\_matrix)] }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \DecValTok{0}

\hypertarget{customers-will-be-at-different-stage-of-purchase-journey-after-each-conversion.}{%
\paragraph{1. Customers will be at different stage of purchase journey after each conversion.}\label{customers-will-be-at-different-stage-of-purchase-journey-after-each-conversion.}}

First-time buyer's journey will look different from n-times buyer's (e.g., he will not start at website )

You can create your own code to split data into customers in different stages.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\#\#\#\# splitting paths \#\#\#\#\#}
\NormalTok{df\_paths }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_raw }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(customer\_id) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{path\_no =} \FunctionTok{ifelse}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{is.na}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{lag}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{cumsum}\NormalTok{(conversion))), }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\FunctionTok{lag}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{cumsum}\NormalTok{(conversion))) }\SpecialCharTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \CommentTok{\# add the path\textquotesingle{}s serial number by using the lagged cumulative sum of conversion binary marks}
        \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{()}
\FunctionTok{head}\NormalTok{(df\_paths)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # A tibble: 6 x 5
##   customer_id date       channel   conversion path_no
##   <chr>       <date>     <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1 id1         2016-01-02 channel_7          0       1
## 2 id1         2016-01-09 channel_4          0       1
## 3 id1         2016-01-18 channel_5          1       1
## 4 id1         2016-01-20 channel_4          1       2
## 5 id100       2016-01-01 channel_0          0       1
## 6 id100       2016-01-01 channel_0          0       1
\end{verbatim}

attribution path for first-time buyers:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{df\_paths\_1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_paths }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(path\_no }\SpecialCharTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{path\_no)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\hypertarget{handle-missing-data}{%
\paragraph{2. Handle missing data}\label{handle-missing-data}}

We might have missing data on the channel or do not want to attribute a path (e.g., Direct Channel). We can either

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Remove NA/Channel
\item
  Use the previous channel in its place.
\end{itemize}

In the first-order Markov chains, the results are unchanged because duplicated channels don't affect the calculation.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\#\#\#\# replace some channels \#\#\#\#\#}
\NormalTok{df\_path\_1\_clean }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_paths\_1 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \CommentTok{\# removing NAs}
        \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{!}\FunctionTok{is.na}\NormalTok{(channel)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
         
        \CommentTok{\# adding order of channels in the path}
        \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(customer\_id) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{ord =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\FunctionTok{n}\NormalTok{()),}
               \AttributeTok{is\_non\_direct =} \FunctionTok{ifelse}\NormalTok{(channel }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}channel\_6\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{),}
               \AttributeTok{is\_non\_direct\_cum =} \FunctionTok{cumsum}\NormalTok{(is\_non\_direct)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
         
        \CommentTok{\# removing Direct (channel\_6) when it is the first in the path}
        \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(is\_non\_direct\_cum }\SpecialCharTok{!=} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
         
        \CommentTok{\# replacing Direct (channel\_6) with the previous touch point}
        \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{channel =} \FunctionTok{ifelse}\NormalTok{(channel }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}channel\_6\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, channel[}\FunctionTok{which}\NormalTok{(channel }\SpecialCharTok{!=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}channel\_6\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)][is\_non\_direct\_cum], channel)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
         
        \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ord, }\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{is\_non\_direct, }\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{is\_non\_direct\_cum)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\hypertarget{one-vs.-multi-channel-paths}{%
\paragraph{3. one vs.~multi-channel paths}\label{one-vs.-multi-channel-paths}}

We need to calculate the weighted importance for each channel because the sum of the Removal Effects doesn't equal to 1. In case we have a path with a unique channel, the Removal Effect and importance of this channel for that exact path is 1. However, weighting with other multi-channel paths will decrease the importance of one-channel occurrences. That means that, in case we have a channel that occurs in one-channel paths, usually it will be underestimated if attributed with multi-channel paths.

There is also a pretty straight logic behind splitting -- for one-channel paths, we definitely know the channel that brought a conversion and we don't need to distribute that value into other channels.

To account for one-channel path:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Split data for paths with one or more unique channels
\item
  Calculate total conversions for one-channel paths and compute the Markov model for multi-channel paths
\item
  Summarize results for each channel.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\#\#\#\# one{-} and multi{-}channel paths \#\#\#\#\#}
\NormalTok{df\_path\_1\_clean }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_path\_1\_clean }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(customer\_id) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{uniq\_channel\_tag =} \FunctionTok{ifelse}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{length}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{unique}\NormalTok{(channel)) }\SpecialCharTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{, }\ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{()}
 
\NormalTok{df\_path\_1\_clean\_uniq }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_path\_1\_clean }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(uniq\_channel\_tag }\SpecialCharTok{==} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{uniq\_channel\_tag)}
 
\NormalTok{df\_path\_1\_clean\_multi }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_path\_1\_clean }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(uniq\_channel\_tag }\SpecialCharTok{==} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{uniq\_channel\_tag)}
 
\DocumentationTok{\#\#\# experiment }\AlertTok{\#\#\#}
\CommentTok{\# attribution model for all paths}
\NormalTok{df\_all\_paths }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_path\_1\_clean }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(customer\_id) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{path =} \FunctionTok{paste}\NormalTok{(channel, }\AttributeTok{collapse =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{} \textgreater{} \textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{),}
                  \AttributeTok{conversion =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(conversion)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(conversion }\SpecialCharTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
 
\NormalTok{mod\_attrib }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{markov\_model}\NormalTok{(df\_all\_paths,}
                           \AttributeTok{var\_path =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}path\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}
                           \AttributeTok{var\_conv =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}conversion\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}
                           \AttributeTok{out\_more =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\NormalTok{df\_multi\_paths }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_path\_1\_clean\_multi }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(customer\_id) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{path =} \FunctionTok{paste}\NormalTok{(channel, }\AttributeTok{collapse =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{} \textgreater{} \textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{),}

\hypertarget{higher-order-markov-chains}{%
\paragraph{4. Higher Order Markov Chains}\label{higher-order-markov-chains}}

Since the transition matrix stays the same in the first order Markov, having duplicates will not affect the result. But starting from the second order order Markov, you will have different results when skipping duplicates. In order to check the effect of skipping duplicates in the first-order Markov chain, we will use my script for ``manual'' calculation because the package skips duplicates automatically.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\#\#\#\# Higher order of Markov chains and consequent duplicated channels in the path \#\#\#\#\#}
 
\CommentTok{\# computing transition matrix {-} \textquotesingle{}manual\textquotesingle{} way}
\NormalTok{df\_multi\_paths\_m }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_multi\_paths }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{path =} \FunctionTok{paste0}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(start) \textgreater{} \textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, path, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{} \textgreater{} (conversion)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{m }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{max}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{str\_count}\NormalTok{(df\_multi\_paths\_m}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{path, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}\textgreater{}\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{+} \DecValTok{1} \CommentTok{\# maximum path length}
 
\NormalTok{df\_multi\_paths\_cols }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ reshape2}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{colsplit}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{string =}\NormalTok{ df\_multi\_paths\_m}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{path, }\AttributeTok{pattern =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{} \textgreater{} \textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{names =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{m))}
\FunctionTok{colnames}\NormalTok{(df\_multi\_paths\_cols) }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{paste0}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}ord\_\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{m))}
\NormalTok{df\_multi\_paths\_cols[df\_multi\_paths\_cols }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \ConstantTok{NA}
 
\NormalTok{df\_res }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{vector}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}list\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\FunctionTok{ncol}\NormalTok{(df\_multi\_paths\_cols) }\SpecialCharTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
 
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ (i }\ControlFlowTok{in} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{ncol}\NormalTok{(df\_multi\_paths\_cols) }\SpecialCharTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))) \{}
         
\NormalTok{        df\_cache }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_multi\_paths\_cols }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{num\_range}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"ord\_"}\NormalTok{, }\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(i, i}\SpecialCharTok{+}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{na.omit}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{group\_by\_}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{.dot =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{paste0}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"ord\_"}\NormalTok{, }\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(i, i}\SpecialCharTok{+}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)))) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{n =} \FunctionTok{n}\NormalTok{()) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{()}
         
        \FunctionTok{colnames}\NormalTok{(df\_cache)[}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)] }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}channel\_from\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}channel\_to\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{        df\_res[[i]] }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_cache}
\NormalTok{\}}
 
\NormalTok{df\_res }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{do.call}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}rbind\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, df\_res)}
 
\NormalTok{df\_res\_tot }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_res }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(channel\_from, channel\_to) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{n =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(n)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(channel\_from) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{tot\_n =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(n),}
               \AttributeTok{perc =}\NormalTok{ n }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ tot\_n) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{()}
 
\NormalTok{df\_dummy }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{channel\_from =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(start)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(conversion)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(null)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{),}
                       \AttributeTok{channel\_to =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(start)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(conversion)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(null)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{),}
                       \AttributeTok{n =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{),}
                       \AttributeTok{tot\_n =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{),}
                       \AttributeTok{perc =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}
 
\NormalTok{df\_res\_tot }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{rbind}\NormalTok{(df\_res\_tot, df\_dummy)}
 
\CommentTok{\# comparing transition matrices}
\NormalTok{trans\_matrix\_prob\_m }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{dcast}\NormalTok{(df\_res\_tot, channel\_from }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ channel\_to, }\AttributeTok{value.var =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}perc\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{fun.aggregate =}\NormalTok{ sum)}
\NormalTok{trans\_matrix\_prob }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(mod\_attrib\_alt}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{transition\_matrix)}
\NormalTok{trans\_matrix\_prob }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{dcast}\NormalTok{(trans\_matrix\_prob, channel\_from }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ channel\_to, }\AttributeTok{value.var =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}transition\_probability\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
 
\CommentTok{\# computing attribution {-} \textquotesingle{}manual\textquotesingle{} way}
\NormalTok{channels\_list }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_path\_1\_clean\_multi }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(conversion }\SpecialCharTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{distinct}\NormalTok{(channel)}
\NormalTok{channels\_list }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(channels\_list}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{channel)}
 
\NormalTok{df\_res\_ini }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_res\_tot }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(channel\_from, channel\_to)}
\NormalTok{df\_attrib }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{vector}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}list\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\FunctionTok{length}\NormalTok{(channels\_list))}
 
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ (i }\ControlFlowTok{in} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\FunctionTok{length}\NormalTok{(channels\_list))) \{}
         
\NormalTok{        channel }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ channels\_list[i]}
         
\NormalTok{        df\_res1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_res }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{channel\_from =} \FunctionTok{ifelse}\NormalTok{(channel\_from }\SpecialCharTok{==}\NormalTok{ channel, }\ConstantTok{NA}\NormalTok{, channel\_from),}
                       \AttributeTok{channel\_to =} \FunctionTok{ifelse}\NormalTok{(channel\_to }\SpecialCharTok{==}\NormalTok{ channel, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(null)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, channel\_to)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{na.omit}\NormalTok{()}
         
\NormalTok{        df\_res\_tot1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_res1 }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(channel\_from, channel\_to) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{n =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(n)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                 
                \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(channel\_from) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{tot\_n =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(n),}
                       \AttributeTok{perc =}\NormalTok{ n }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ tot\_n) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
                \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{()}
         
\NormalTok{        df\_res\_tot1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{rbind}\NormalTok{(df\_res\_tot1, df\_dummy) }\CommentTok{\# adding (start), (conversion) and (null) states}
         
\NormalTok{        df\_res\_tot1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{left\_join}\NormalTok{(df\_res\_ini, df\_res\_tot1, }\AttributeTok{by =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}channel\_from\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}channel\_to\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{        df\_res\_tot1[}\FunctionTok{is.na}\NormalTok{(df\_res\_tot1)] }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \DecValTok{0}
         
\NormalTok{        df\_trans1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{dcast}\NormalTok{(df\_res\_tot1, channel\_from }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ channel\_to, }\AttributeTok{value.var =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}perc\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{fun.aggregate =}\NormalTok{ sum)}
         
\NormalTok{        trans\_matrix\_1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_trans1}

\NormalTok{        inist\_n1[}\FunctionTok{is.na}\NormalTok{(inist\_n1)] }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \DecValTok{0}
\NormalTok{        inist\_n1 }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ inist\_n1[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}(start)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, ]}

\NormalTok{        df\_cache }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{channel\_name =}\NormalTok{ channel,}

\NormalTok{        df\_attrib[[i]] }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_cache}
\NormalTok{\}}
 
\NormalTok{df\_attrib }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{do.call}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}rbind\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, df\_attrib)}
 
\CommentTok{\# computing removal effect and results}
\NormalTok{tot\_conv }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(df\_multi\_paths\_m}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{conversion)}
 
\NormalTok{df\_attrib }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_attrib }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{tot\_conversions =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(df\_multi\_paths\_m}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{conversion),}
               \AttributeTok{impact =}\NormalTok{ (tot\_conversions }\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ conversions) }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ tot\_conversions,}
               \AttributeTok{tot\_impact =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(impact),}
               \AttributeTok{weighted\_impact =}\NormalTok{ impact }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ tot\_impact,}
               \AttributeTok{attrib\_model\_conversions =} \FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(tot\_conversions }\SpecialCharTok{*}\NormalTok{ weighted\_impact)}
\NormalTok{        ) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
        \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(channel\_name, attrib\_model\_conversions)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since with different transition matrices, the removal effects and attribution results stay the same, in practice we skip duplicates.

\hypertarget{non-conversion-paths}{%

In conclusion, we say that if a customer made contact with a marketing channel the first time for more than 23 days and/or hasn't made contact with a marketing channel for the last 12 days, then it is a fruitless path.

        \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{path =} \FunctionTok{paste}\NormalTok{(channel, }\AttributeTok{collapse =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{} \textgreater{} \textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{),}
                  \AttributeTok{tot\_time\_lapse =} \FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{as.numeric}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{max}\NormalTok{(date) }\SpecialCharTok{{-}} \FunctionTok{min}\NormalTok{(date))),}

\hypertarget{channel-comparisons}{%
\paragraph{7. Channel Comparisons}\label{channel-comparisons}}

We can use \texttt{markov\_model} with \texttt{var\_value} to compare the gross margin among channels.

\hypertarget{example-3}{%
\subsubsection{Example 3}\label{example-3}}

This example is from \href{https://www.bounteous.com/insights/2016/06/30/marketing-channel-attribution-markov-models-r/}{Bounteus}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Install these libraries (only do this once)}
\CommentTok{\# install.packages("ChannelAttribution")}
\CommentTok{\# install.packages("reshape")}
\CommentTok{\# install.packages("ggplot2")}

\CommentTok{\# Load these libraries (every time you start RStudio)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(ChannelAttribution)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(reshape)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(ggplot2)}

\CommentTok{\# This loads the demo data. You can load your own data by importing a dataset or reading in a file}
\FunctionTok{data}\NormalTok{(PathData)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Path Variable -- The steps a user takes across sessions to comprise the sequences.
\item
  Conversion Variable -- How many times a user converted.
\item
  Value Variable -- The monetary value of each marketing channel.
\item
  Null Variable -- How many times a user exited.
\end{itemize}

Build the simple heuristic models (First Click / first\_touch, Last Click / last\_touch, and Linear Attribution / linear\_touch):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{heuristic\_models}\NormalTok{(Data, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}path\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}total\_conversions\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{var\_value=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}total\_conversion\_value\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## [1] "*** Looking to run more advanced attribution? Try ChannelAttribution Pro for free! Visit https://channelattribution.io/product"
\end{verbatim}

Markov model

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{markov\_model}\NormalTok{(Data, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}path\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}total\_conversions\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{var\_value=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}total\_conversion\_value\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{order =} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## 
## Number of simulations: 100000 - Convergence reached: 1.46% < 5.00%
## 
## Percentage of simulated paths that successfully end before maximum number of steps (46) is reached: 99.99%

\hypertarget{sales-funnel}{%
\section{Sales Funnel}\label{sales-funnel}}

\hypertarget{example-1-1}{%
\subsection{Example 1}\label{example-1-1}}

This example is based on \href{https://www.analyzecore.com/2017/09/28/marketing-multi-channel-attribution-model-based-on-sales-funnel-with-r/}{Sergey Bryl}

\[
Awareness \to Interest \to Desire \to Action 
\]

Step in the funnel:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  0 step (necessary condition) -- customer visits a site for the first time
\item
  1st step (awareness) -- visits two site's pages
\item
  2nd step (interest) -- reviews a product page
\item
  3rd step (desire) -- adds a product to the shopping cart
\item
  4th step (action) -- completes purchase
\end{itemize}

Preprocessing

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\#\# removing not first events }\AlertTok{\#\#\#}
\NormalTok{df\_customers }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_raw }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(customer\_id, event) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(date }\SpecialCharTok{==} \FunctionTok{min}\NormalTok{(date)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Assumption: all customers are first-time buyers. Hence, every next purchase as an event will be removed with the above code.

Calculate channel probability

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\#\# Sales Funnel probabilities }\AlertTok{\#\#\#}
\NormalTok{sf\_probs }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_customers }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    
    \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(event) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{customers\_on\_step =} \FunctionTok{n}\NormalTok{()) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    
    \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}
        \AttributeTok{sf\_probs =} \FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(customers\_on\_step }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ customers\_on\_step[event }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}site\_visit\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
        \AttributeTok{sf\_probs\_step =} \FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(customers\_on\_step }\SpecialCharTok{/} \FunctionTok{lag}\NormalTok{(customers\_on\_step), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
        \AttributeTok{sf\_probs\_step =} \FunctionTok{ifelse}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{is.na}\NormalTok{(sf\_probs\_step) }\SpecialCharTok{==} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, sf\_probs\_step),}
        \AttributeTok{sf\_importance =} \DecValTok{1} \SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ sf\_probs\_step,}
        \AttributeTok{sf\_importance\_weighted =}\NormalTok{ sf\_importance }\SpecialCharTok{/} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(sf\_importance)}
\NormalTok{    )}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Calculate attribution

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\DocumentationTok{\#\#\# computing attribution }\AlertTok{\#\#\#}
\NormalTok{df\_attrib }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df\_customers }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \CommentTok{\# removing customers without purchase}
    \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(customer\_id) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{any}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{as.character}\NormalTok{(event) }\SpecialCharTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}purchase\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    
    \CommentTok{\# joining step\textquotesingle{}s importances}
    \FunctionTok{left\_join}\NormalTok{(., sf\_probs }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{select}\NormalTok{(event, sf\_importance\_weighted), }\AttributeTok{by =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}event\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    
    \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(channel) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{tot\_attribution =} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(sf\_importance\_weighted)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\hypertarget{rfm}{%
\section{RFM}\label{rfm}}

\href{https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rfm/vignettes/rfm-customer-level-data.html}{RFM} is calculated as:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  A recency score is assigned to each customer based on date of most recent purchase.
\item
  A frequency ranking is assigned based on frequency of purchases
\item
  Monetary score is assigned based on the total revenue generated by the customer in the period under consideration for the analysis
\end{itemize}

\hypertarget{rfmc}{%
\subsection{RFMC}\label{rfmc}}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\Alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  clumpiness is defined as the degree of nonconformity to equal spacing \citep{Zhang_2015}
\end{enumerate}

In finance, clumpiness can indicate high growth potential but large risk, Hence, it can be incorporated into firm acquisition decision. Originated from sports phenomenon - hot hand effect - where success leads to more success.

In statistics, clumpiness is the serial dependence or ``non-constant propensity, specifically temporary elevations of propensity--- i.e.~periods during which one event is more likely to occur than the average level.'' \citep{Zhang_2013}

Properties of clumpiness:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Min (max) if events are equally spaced (close to one another)
\item
  Continuity
\item
  Convergence
\end{itemize}

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  campaign, which includes campaign name and customer acquisition cost for each customer,
\item
  margin, which includes gross margin for each product,
\item
  potential, which includes potential values / predicted CLV for each client,
\item
  orders, which includes orders from our customers with products and order dates.
\end{itemize}

\NormalTok{    reshape2}\SpecialCharTok{::}\FunctionTok{melt}\NormalTok{(}
\NormalTok{        cohorts,}

\hypertarget{shopping-carts-analysis}{%
\section{Shopping carts analysis}\label{shopping-carts-analysis}}

\hypertarget{multi-layer-pie-chart}{%
\subsection{Multi-layer pie chart}\label{multi-layer-pie-chart}}

Example by \href{https://www.analyzecore.com/2014/10/17/cart-analysis-r/}{Sergey Bryl}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# loading libraries}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(dplyr)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(tidyverse)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(reshape2)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(plotrix)}

\CommentTok{\# Simulate of orders}
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{df }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}
    \AttributeTok{orderId =} \FunctionTok{sample}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{), }\DecValTok{5000}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{replace =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{),}
    \AttributeTok{product =} \FunctionTok{sample}\NormalTok{(}
        \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}NULL\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}a\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}b\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}c\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}d\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{),}
        \DecValTok{5000}\NormalTok{,}
        \AttributeTok{replace =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{,}
        \AttributeTok{prob =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\FloatTok{0.15}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.65}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.15}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    )}
\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{df }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df[df}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{product }\SpecialCharTok{!=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}NULL\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,]}
\FunctionTok{head}\NormalTok{(df)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
##   orderId product
## 1     549       b
## 3     874       a
## 4     674       d
## 5     505       a
## 6     294       a
## 7     177       a
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# processing initial data}
\CommentTok{\# we need to be sure that product\textquotesingle{}s names are unique}
\NormalTok{df}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{product }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{paste0}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"\#"}\NormalTok{, df}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{product, }\StringTok{"\#"}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{prod.matrix }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ df }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \CommentTok{\# removing duplicated products from each order (exclude the effect of quantity)}
    \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(orderId, product) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{arrange}\NormalTok{(product) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{unique}\NormalTok{() }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \CommentTok{\# combining products to cart and calculating number of products}
    \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(orderId) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{cart =} \FunctionTok{paste}\NormalTok{(product, }\AttributeTok{collapse =} \StringTok{";"}\NormalTok{),}
              \AttributeTok{prod.num =} \FunctionTok{n}\NormalTok{()) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \CommentTok{\# calculating number of carts}
    \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(cart, prod.num) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{summarise}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{num =} \FunctionTok{n}\NormalTok{()) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{ungroup}\NormalTok{()}

\FunctionTok{head}\NormalTok{(prod.matrix)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## # A tibble: 6 x 3
##   cart            prod.num   num
##   <chr>              <int> <int>
## 1 #a#                    1   115
## 2 #a#;#b#                2   248
## 3 #a#;#b#;#c#            3   172
## 4 #a#;#b#;#c#;#d#        4    78
## 5 #a#;#b#;#d#            3   119
## 6 #a#;#c#                2    98
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# calculating total number of orders/carts}
\NormalTok{tot }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(prod.matrix}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{num)}

\CommentTok{\# spliting orders for sets with 1 product and more than 1 product}
\NormalTok{one.prod }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ prod.matrix }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(prod.num }\SpecialCharTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{sev.prod }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ prod.matrix }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(prod.num }\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
    \FunctionTok{arrange}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{desc}\NormalTok{(prod.num))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# defining parameters for pie chart}
\NormalTok{iniR }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FloatTok{0.2} \CommentTok{\# initial radius}
\NormalTok{cols }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}
    \StringTok{"\#ffffff"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"\#fec44f"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"\#fc9272"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"\#a1d99b"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"\#fee0d2"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"\#2ca25f"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"\#8856a7"}\NormalTok{,}

\hypertarget{sequence-in-depth-analysis}{%
\subsection{Sequence in-depth analysis}\label{sequence-in-depth-analysis}}

Example by \href{https://www.analyzecore.com/2014/12/04/sequence-carts-in-depth-analysis-with-r/}{Sergey Bryl}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  To understand customer's behavior and churn based on purchase sequence. For example,

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    If the customer has left or did not make the next purchase
  \item
    Understand duration between purchases
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(dplyr)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(TraMineR)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(reshape2)}
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(googleVis)}

\CommentTok{\# creating an example of shopping carts}
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{data }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}
    \AttributeTok{orderId =} \FunctionTok{sample}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{), }\DecValTok{5000}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{replace =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{),}
    \AttributeTok{product =} \FunctionTok{sample}\NormalTok{(}
        \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}NULL\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}a\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}b\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}c\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{), }\CommentTok{\# assume we have only 3 products }
        \DecValTok{5000}\NormalTok{,}
        \AttributeTok{replace =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{,}
        \AttributeTok{prob =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\FloatTok{0.15}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.65}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.15}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    )}
\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# we also know customers\textquotesingle{} purchase order }
\NormalTok{order }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{orderId =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{),}
                    \AttributeTok{clientId =} \FunctionTok{sample}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{300}\NormalTok{), }\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{replace =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{))}

\CommentTok{\# suppose we know customers\textquotesingle{} gender}
\NormalTok{sex }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{clientId =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{300}\NormalTok{),}
                  \AttributeTok{sex =} \FunctionTok{sample}\NormalTok{(}
                      \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}male\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}female\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{),}
                      \DecValTok{300}\NormalTok{,}
                      \AttributeTok{replace =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{,}
                      \AttributeTok{prob =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\FloatTok{0.40}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.60}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{                  ))}


\NormalTok{date }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{orderId =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{),}
                   \AttributeTok{orderdate =} \FunctionTok{sample}\NormalTok{((}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{90}\NormalTok{), }\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{replace =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{orders }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{merge}\NormalTok{(data, order, }\AttributeTok{by =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}orderId\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{orders }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{merge}\NormalTok{(orders, sex, }\AttributeTok{by =} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}clientId\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{orders }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ orders[orders}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{product }\SpecialCharTok{!=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}NULL\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,]}
\NormalTok{orders}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{orderdate }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{as.Date}\NormalTok{(orders}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{orderdate, }\AttributeTok{origin =} \StringTok{"2012{-}01{-}01"}\NormalTok{)}
\FunctionTok{rm}\NormalTok{(data, date, order, sex)}

\FunctionTok{head}\NormalTok{(orders)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\NormalTok{          clientId }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ ord,}
